Title: Maus I: A Survivor's Tale: My Father Bleeds History (Maus, #1)
Author: Art Spiegelman
My Review:
Five stars for an amazing book. Either comic books get brushed off by dedicated readers, or are exclusively read by those who normally hate books; impressively, this book will can be a comfortable fit for comic-book readers and non-comic book readers alike.

This story provides us not just the facts about the Holocaust in the book, but a methodical chronology of the emotions that a particular family experiences throughout the war.

In addition, because of this book, I better the process of parenthood and how growing up can affect what you become as a parent. From this story, for example, we learn that Vladek, the narrator's (Artie's) dad has an unexplicable tendency to save any money he makes. However, out of the love for his son, he will always provide anything his son asks for.

As for the length of the book (this being part I), the plot will never tire you and there are natural pauses for the reader. This is directly because the artist himself is taking breaks from writing his father's biography. Fortunately, Spiegelman allows the story to flow on its own, as if the words had a life of their own.

Title: The Call of Cthulhu
Author: H.P. Lovecraft
My Review:
The Call of Cthulhu is a short story written by H.P. Lovecraft first published in 1926. The story follows a secretive investigation by the nephew of a linguistics professor called Mr. Angell. After the death of his uncle, the narrator studies a series of coincidental evidence suggesting the existence of an ancient and unknown nightmarish Cyclopean city with a creature called the Cthulhu.

The story relates different pieces of evidence, such as a sculpture from an art student called Wilcox, as well as the finding of a cult which claimed to worship gods called "Great Old Ones". Upon reading a clipping from an Australian newspaper, Thurston, the narrator, contacts the widow of a man who had died after a boat trip to an uncharted island. The manuscript of this man reveals that the man and the crew had accidentally released the Cthulhu.

The most striking detail of the story comes from the description of the city the boat crew disappears on. The "non-Euclidean" geometry upon which the city is formed easily disturbs any reader in a way that traditional horror would not achieve.

Although the story can be tedious in the study of evidence, the final chapter, in which the manuscript reveals all about the Cthulhu is worth the wait.

Title: A Brief History of Time
Author: Stephen Hawking
My Review:
A Brief History of Time was originally published in 1988. The main theme of the book is exploring the origin and future of our universe, and analysis of the laws that currently predict the events around us. Stephen Hawking has been described as the most prominent physicist since Einstein and had the goal of explaining to the non-scientific community the most recent developments in our understanding of the universe. Hawking's main point in this book is that understanding our world with one unified theorem is something that would be worth seeking, since he believes strongly in its possible existence as well as the ability of human intelligence to discover it. While Stephen Hawking intended any person to grasp the mathematical and physical structures of our universe, I believe that only at a college graduate level at minimum could grasp these ideas; I felt most at loss when the kinds of elementary particles came to be discussed: quarks, leptons, and bosons. Hawking discusses physics and both macro- and minuscule levels, leaving me most confused at times when the reader encountered particles and spin.

Certain sections were totally unexpected, like Chapter 11 - The Unification of Physics, when he starts describing string theory. I certainly never even heard a whisper of string theory from my physics teachers in high school, only recalling that my sister's entrance essay to University of Chicago briefly asked her to comment on "string theory". The theory itself must have certainly been important at the time, but I can't help but feeling like the theory is no longer worth including.

The most delightful chapter is probably Chapter 9, when we learn about why entropy (disorder) increases over time. All of our world is like a jigsaw puzzle, and as time goes on, the box holding the jigsaw puzzle can be thought of as "shaken". Therefore, a thousand possibilities of mixed up pieces is more likely for the puzzle than one put together set. Humans would have needed entropy for the way we consume fuel and Hawking believes we believe we exist in part to entropy and therefore what we see for our universe is ever increasing entropy.

Some of the overly repeated ideas I believe are the weak and strong anthropic principles; that was probably the most logically weak idea of the book! This mumble-jumble that was trying to understand this is still hard for me to process: where weak I think meant us humans happening to believe the world works the way it does, because if it didn't we would be alive to observe that, and where strong meant some higher being made lots of different universes so that one of us could exist in a habitable version.

Another idea that was emphasized with utmost importance was the uncertainty principle, which was described as having unknown both the momentum and position of a particle at any one time. Although mentioned a lot in the book, I felt that there was no one chapter in particular that went into depth about it, in order to merit it's assumption in later chapters.

This book is amazing for having refreshed all my memory of physics from high school, and combining ideas I heard in physics as well as in biology. I agree with Hawking, in that the quest for a unified theorem is one worth accepting, as nothing would be more fulfilling for humanity than having satisfied our thirst for understanding the true cause and design of our universe.

Title: The Monk of Mokha
Author: Dave Eggers
My Review:
The Monk of Mokha by Dave Eggers follows the true story of Mokhtar Alkhanshali, a Yemeni American who is determined to start a unique coffee export business from Yemen during the midst of a civil war. While travelling to Yemen, he gathers coffee samples and explores the history of the region all the while surviving confrontations with both Houthis and Saudis.

Mokhtar himself is an inspiring example of someone who despite a lack of college degree, found his passion and dedicated himself wholeheartedley to it, finding success by way of his strong determination. When having failed the Q grader certification the first time, but having passed many sections, he exclaimed that he hadn't scored as high on an exam since middle school, showing resiliency.

This novel is a careful account of one man's journey to culinary excellence in the area of coffee. The plot reads like an action novel, and includes fascinating details about San Francisco and Yemeni culture. However, I at times would have liked to know more about the history of the civil war in Yemen, having it be such a central part of the second half of the book.

Title: Winston Churchill: A Life From Beginning to End (World War 2 Biographies)
Author: Hourly History
My Review:
Winston Churchill: A Life From Beginning to End is a short biography by Hourly History, self-described as a publishing group that provides concise, straightforward and takes no longer than one hour to read. This book provides an excellent condensation of the life story of Winston Churchill from birth to death, providing facts about his personal military adventures as a soldier and then as a war reporter, and later progression in political ranks in England. The only thing lacking from this book was a view into the more controversial aspects of his leadership.

The most interesting role Winston Churchill had to play was in the final plans for the invasion of France, known as Operation Overlord. Churchill noted that the closest launching point across the Channel was in Dover, directly across from Pas de Calais, but that Pas de Calais had been fortified by the Germans. The Normandy landing sight, however, provided a broader platform for maneuver. Tthe Battle of Normandy, which lasted from June 1944 to August 1944, resulted in the Allied liberation of Western Europe from Nazi Germany’s control.

Churchill after claiming a victory of France, he tried to bargain with Stalin before the Soviet capture of the remaining European countries. During a his farewell address after losing reelection, he gave his famous "Iron Curtain" speech, stating that Soviet domination seemed to be spreading. Churchill appeared to be genuinely concerned with Stalin's plans of conquest, but when seen dealing was Stalin, was viewed as promoting British imperialism. To bolster the strength of Western Europe, he had the idea to create the European Union. The union that Churchill dreamed of was one that a free Europe would voluntarily join out of a mutual desire to work together. In addition, Churchill notably stepped in during May of 1945 when the French attempted to regain the territory in Syria and Lebanon lost during the German occupation.

My Review:
Prequels are opportunities to further add to the world-building of a novel, and [b:The Silmarillion|7332|The Silmarillion|J.R.R. Tolkien|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1610045590l/7332._SX50_.jpg|4733799] by J.R.R. Tolkien certainly provides a complete view of the building of Arda from the creation of Middle Earth up to the time of Frodo Baggins and his quest to destroy the One Ring. The book takes place in five parts: The Ainulindalë (the creation of Eä), the Valaquenta (an introduction to the Valar and the Maiar), The Quenta Silmarillion (the history of the First Age), The Akallabêth (the history of the Second Age) and Of the Rings of Power and the Third Age (the telling of the Third Age). My favorite chapter was “Of Beren and Lúthien”, which tells the tale of how Beren went to Angband to retrieve a Simaril, and shows how fate and determinism allows many characters to overcome much stronger foes.
The purpose of this novel is to be a creation story, and the level of detail provided makes the novel feel like parts of the Bible, specifically the Old Testament. When Middle Earth was created, the almighty creator (Eru Ilúvatar) created angels (Valar & Maiar). However, Melkor, being the most powerful Vala, has a falling out with Iluvatar, and is cast down (like Lucifer). Aule then shaped the dwarves, and Elves and Men were formed from the mind of Iluvatar, called "First" and "Second" Children of Ilúvatar (or Eruhini), respectively.
Some of the strongest characters include Feanor and Earendil. Feanor is the first King of the Noldor, and one of the children of the elves that departed from Valinor. As a gem-smith, he was a maker of the Silmarils, and was granted the most skill of all the Elves. However his pride over the Silmarils grew into greed, as he soon ignored that the beauty of the gems was the light of the Two Trees of Valinor that was captured within them, not the gems on their own. Melkor, being the source of evil, knowing that the Noldor had a thirst for knowledge, used Feanor’s impatience to plant lies and provoke violence in Feanor against his half-brother Fingolfin.
Earendil, on the other hand, is one of the Half-Elven and the patriarch of the line of the Kings of Numenor through his son Elros. He is the first known person to reach Aman (or Valinor) after the Noldor went into exile. Later in Arvernien, much after escaping the fall of Gondolin, he becomes the leader of the people there and marries Elwing, the son of Beren and Luthien. Seeking out his parents Tuor and Idril, he leaves by ship while his people are attacked by the sons of Feanor for holding onto a Simaril. As such, he completes his journey to Valinor to ask for aid for the men and elves of Middle Earth against Morgoth.
The biggest theme of this novel is fate. The struggle against evil, first born in Melkor’s rebellion, takes place during the “First Age” of Middle Earth, which involves not only the Valar, but men, dwarves and elves. The struggle against this evil ends with the demise of Morgoth’s rule over Middle Earth, but the evil continues in the “Second Age” with the rise of Sauron, Morgoth’s most powerful servant. During the “Second Age”, the Numenoreans become increasingly fearful of the darkness around them created by Morgoth and fear death. However, by fighting against the “gift of Death” that Iluvatar granted them by design, they created their own downfall by attempting to make war of the Valar and obtain immortality by force.
[b:The Silmarillion|7332|The Silmarillion|J.R.R. Tolkien|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1610045590l/7332._SX50_.jpg|4733799] by J.R.R. Tolkien bundles together the tricky act of world-building, character development and themes like fate in a way that respects continuity and traditions of fantasy found in earlier novels like The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. The only caveat to such a novel is to take it in small pieces, and read each section slowly, whether as a fountain of moral guidance or for sheer entertainment. While there is a glossary provided with the novel, attempting to read each story consecutively, without stopping, can lead to important causal plot points from being noticed.

My Review:
[b:Putita golosa: por un feminismo del goce|40122791|Putita golosa por un feminismo del goce|Luciana Peker|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1526348521l/40122791._SX50_.jpg|62225424], una novela de Luciana Peker, a primera vista inspira a pensar en la idea feminista de que a las mujeres se les permite disfrutar de su propio placer. En varios capítulos, la autora da ejemplos de cómo el placer de las mujeres ha sido blanco del machismo. Sin embargo, además de este argumento está el cuestionamiento del amor romántico, y el reconocimiento de que el machismo también afecta negativamente a los hombres.

Las mejores partes del libro reconocen que el cambio real debe provenir de hombres que trabajan junto con mujeres, porque sus libertades tambien estan en riesgo. En el capítulo 4 “El amor nuevo”, Luciana argumenta que la educación de los niños no ha cambiado mucho. “Y nadie… prepara a los varones para no ser heroes ni valientes o conquistadores. Y tinenen frente a un escenario completamente diferente.” (pág. 125). De esta forma, es cierto que los hombres también sufren las expectativas sociales de ser algo que no son, o no quieren ser. Al comienzo del capítulo 5 vemos que “el machismo perjudica a las mujeres y, también, perjudica a los varones”. (pág. 131). Como conclusión de este capítulo queda claro que el machismo afecta más a las mujeres que a los hombres, pero sin libertad para las mujeres, no hay libertad para los hombres.

Un argumento interesante del libro es que el amor romántico no necesita ser una necesidad para el amor. En particular, el libro valora el respeto mutuo, citando a Corral Herrer Gomez quien dice que “si no hay reciprocidad, lo mejor es dejar la relacion”. Como muchos lectores probablemente puedan relacionarse, Corral argumenta que es difícil estar con alguien que no te da la misma energía emocional, mental y física que tú das, y que continuar derramando esta energía puede disminuir tu autoestima. Otro argumento en contra del amor romántico es que se ha expresado en la sociedad “que el amor nos va a salvar y nos va a hacer felices” (pág. 148) siendo la monogamia parte obligatoria de esta ecuación para las mujeres, aunque no necesariamente para ellas. hombres. En última instancia, la conclusión es que el amor se puede mostrar en más de un sentido, incluso a través de un abrazo o mostrando vulnerabilidad.

Finalmente, un argumento final que cierra el círculo del libro es que empoderarse con su sexualidad se trata de disfrutar su tiempo y no sentirse en deuda con complacer a la otra persona exclusivamente. En el Capítulo 8 “Amas de casa”, vemos que la tolerancia a menudo se ve como un “juego de suma cero”, de modo que más derechos para el placer de las mujeres deben obtenerse a expensas del placer de los hombres. Para confirmarlo, el autor proporciona algunos ejemplos “ni la quita de impuestos al campo y a la mineria se refleja en mayor empleo o mayores ingresos para la poblacion, ni la exaltacion de mujeres gauchitas derraman varones mas satisfechos” (pg. 171). Además, vemos que hay muchas expectativas sociales que funcionan como restricciones a la libertad de expresión sexual. Por ejemplo “no sentir deseos sexuales no es una enfermedad que encesita de pastillas. Los mimos, caricias, tiempo y palabras pueden producir la magia que esperamos.” (pg. 176). Lo más beneficioso tanto para hombres como para mujeres sería aceptar la sexualidad tal como es: una variedad de experiencias.

[b:Putita golosa: por un feminismo del goce|40122791|Putita golosa por un feminismo del goce|Luciana Peker|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1526348521l/40122791._SX50_.jpg|62225424], si bien inicialmente sirve como un debate a favor del placer femenino, va más allá de este debate para incluir las ideas de que el machismo afecta negativamente a mujeres y hombres, que el amor romántico puede ser restrictivo al obligar al amor a verse de cierta manera y que la sexualidad viene en una variedad de formas, y debe centrarse en el disfrute. El libro incluso va más allá de estos argumentos, tocando varios ejemplos políticos y sociales de la forma en que el feminismo ayudaría a la sociedad a crecer, utilizando a Argentina como telón de fondo único para el debate feminista.

Title: Under the Volcano
Author: Malcolm Lowry
My Review:
Under the Volcano by Malcolm Lowry follows the story of an alcoholic and former British Consul called Geoffrey Firmin who is recently separated from his wife Yvonne. The novel is set Mexico on the Day of the Dead in 1938, in the town of Quauhnahuac – more commonly known as Cuernavaca – that is overlooked by two volcanoes, Popocatepetl and Iztaccihuatl. The novel transcends a linear story line by repeating back to events that happened to Geoffrey a year before, while continuing with the original plot of events that happen within that day. The novel was deeply rich in its descriptions, vocabulary and overall portrayal of emotion, however, keeping track of reality was extremely difficult.

Many scenes in the book are of nightmarish descriptions, creating the sensation that the reader was experiencing hell on earth. The descriptions of the town included the animal life: “small, black, ugly birds, yet too long, something like monstrous insects, something like crows, with awkward long tails, and an undulating, bouncing, labored flight.” (pg. 15). Later on a sense of doom is felt in the town: “darkness had fallen like the House of Usher.” (pg. 26). Finally, in a hotel note found by another character, Geoffrey describes himself as “as a great explorer who has discovered some extraordinary land from which he can never return to give his knowledge to the world: but the name of this land is hell.” (pg. 44).

As the story progresses, we note the European influence on the narrator, who uses French and Italian vocabulary to describe the environment. When one of the employees of a tavern hands M. Laruelle was a book that belonged to the Consul, he recounts that he “listened to the water booming down the gutters beneath the one jalousie door of the Cervecería XX” (pg. 34), as the employee gave an awkward cough, or, “appoggiatura” (pg. 34) – melodic note.

Plenty of emotion is associated with ships in the book, in particular regarding the love the narrator has for Yvonne. When Yvonne meets with Geoffrey again in Cuernavaca, she describes taking a boat to see him because “she would have time on board to persuade herself her journey was neither thoughtless nor precipitate”(pg. 59). This takes place after we find out that the Consul has pleaded for Yvonne to return to him. Later when Yvonne and Geoffrey walk to the house, Yvonne begins to inspect the garden and observes the chaos that surrounds the house. “Nevertheless, repenting her tardy impulse to follow the Consul in, she waited outside, restless as a little yacht turning at anchor. The opportunity to join him ebbed.” (pg. 70). Her reluctance to enter perhaps reflects her reluctance to enter back into the relationship.

The novel is a beautiful revelation of the precariousness of humanity in a chaotic world, at times referring to the location of the novel as “hell on earth” and a place full of emotional, particularly representative of the chaotic end of WW2, around the time the book was published. The use of ominous descriptions, European vocabulary and metaphors creates a rich feeling of being inside the mind of the narrator, although at times, totally disconnected from reality.

[b:Parable of the Sower|52397|Parable of the Sower (Earthseed, #1)|Octavia E. Butler|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1442169447l/52397._SY75_.jpg|59258] by [a:Octavia E. Butler|29535|Octavia E. Butler|https://images.gr-assets.com/authors/1242244143p2/29535.jpg] is the first part of a two-book series that takes place in 2024, with a young girl called Lauren Olamina living in her father's community in a disease and drug-ridden United States that is falling apart due to chaotic social and economic change. After her community is attacked, Lauren is forced to escape up North, founding her own religion, Earthseed along the way.

The most incredible part of the book is the wonderful world-building that takes place. A lot of detail is centered on Lauren’s complicated relationship to family, and her desire to move beyond the comforts of her family unit for survival purposes. Lauren is described as really caring for her dad, stating “he’s the best person I know, and I care what he thinks. I wish I didn’t but I do.” (location 348). Lauren likely admires her dad’s diligence in caring for the family, even when he has used corporal punishment on Lauren in the past.

Another interesting aspect of the book is the fact that the story follows entries in Lauren’s diary, which serves as a coping mechanism. Lauren’s mother abused drugs, causing Lauren to be born with hyperempathy syndrome. Lauren uses her journal to talk about pain that she doesn’t feel safe sharing with others: “Sometimes I write to keep from going crazy. There’s a world of things I don’t feel free to talk to anyone about” (location 708). Lauren’s syndrome causes her to feel pain and joy as the people around her do, making it difficult for her to separate out her feelings from the people around her. In writing, Lauren sees fit that “Clarity and truth will be plenty, if I can only achieve them.” (location 1746).

Lauren’s journal entries also serve as a draft for the new religion she is creating, called Earthseed. Interestingly, the religion does not center on an authority figure, but rather the power of individual communities to adapt and survive. “Earthseed deals with ongoing reality, not with supernatural authority figures. Worship is no good without action. With action, it’s only useful if it steadies you, focuses your efforts, eases your mind” (location 3132). In this sense, Lauren designs her religion to be very functional, such that practicing her religion means creating meaningful work rather than blindly following the word of a higher power.

[b:Parable of the Sower|52397|Parable of the Sower (Earthseed, #1)|Octavia E. Butler|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1442169447l/52397._SY75_.jpg|59258] is an incredible look into the world-view of an 18-year old girl called Lauren who is growing up in a country that has broken down into dystopian decay. Through the power of her social network and her own writing, Lauren is simultaneously able to break free from the confines of her family, but also provide a safe haven for other survivors and refuges of a dangerous and violent world.

Title: Boquitas pintadas
Author: Manuel Puig
My Review:
[b:Boquitas pintadas|1292907|Boquitas pintadas|Manuel Puig|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1182545049l/1292907._SY75_.jpg|957471] de [a:Manuel Puig|35548|Manuel Puig|https://images.gr-assets.com/authors/1387957776p2/35548.jpg] es una novela que tiene lugar en 1937 y termina varios años después en 1968. El libro se enfoca en el triangulo de amor entre Juan Carlos, un mujeriego, Nené su gran amor que lo rechaza por un hombre con más plata, y Mabel que pasa tiempo con Juan Carlos pero es tan infiel como él. La primera parte del libro “Boquitas Pintadas de Rojo Carmesí”. Juan Carlos se enferma con tuberculosis y tiene que recibir tratamiento en una pensión en Cordoba. La historia de los personajes se conoce por las cartas que se envían principalmente entre Nene y Leonor Saldívar, pero después entre Nene y Juan Carlos, y finalmente Nene y Celina, la hermana de Juan Carlos. El libro es casi dedicado a recordar el enamoramiento juvenil y permite al lector identificar lo sentimental en lo real, de manera que las emociones toman gran importancia frente a un trasfondo bastante aburrido de un pueblo periférico y tareas domesticas. Por enfocarse en lo sentimental, no me gustó el cuento, ya que todos los personajes tienen motivaciones emocionales muy fuertes y muy incomodas de observar.

El libro muestra bien la jerarquía social de los habitantes del pueblo Coronel Vallejos. Juan Carlos y Pancho, por ejemplo, hablan de lo lindo que es la piel blanca sobre otros colores de piel, mostrando un racismo heredado de las creencias de esa época. Nené por ejemplo, toma su decisión de casarse con Massa, a pesar de faltar de atributos físicos, pero sabiendo que él tiene plata para satisfacer a sus placeres. Finalmente, se nota una falta de respeto general Raba, que fue a la escuela con Nené, Mabel y Celina y tiene hijo con Pancho. Aunque Pancho tuvo hijo con Raba, no lo reconoce como su hijo. Todas las formas en que actúan los personajes suelen basarse en la posición que ocupa cada uno con respecto a otras clases sociales.

Lo lindo del libro es el medio que haya elegido Puig en elaborar la historia. A partir de cartas, descripciones de objetos de casa, y lugares, Puig logra mostrar los pensamientos reales de sus personajes sin que esas personas tengan que interactuar con otros personajes de manera directa. En este sentido el exceso emocional que muestra el libro no está limitado al dialogo como artefacto narrativo, si no que Puig incorpora el tratamiento del sentir como artefacto principal.

Al final, Boquitas Pintadas se lee como una expresión de los deseos de personajes entre varios niveles socioeconómicos con motivaciones distintas, pero todos capturados con lo que es el amor juvenil. El formato de cartas organiza los pensamientos en una estructura bastante adictiva de seguir, pero termina abrumando al lector que se pierde en las fantasías y los chismes de un pequeño pueblo.

Title: El beso de la mujer araña

My Review:
[b:El beso de la mujer araña|63219|El beso de la mujer araña|Manuel Puig|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1386920300l/63219._SY75_.jpg|765288] es un increíble reflejo de los limites de dolor y amor que cruza el humano en situaciones extremas. Dos prisioneros habitan la misma celda, uno por haber "corruptado" un menor y otro por ser parte de un grupo revolucionario. Molina se desarolla como un compañero muy cuidador de su amigo, mientras Valentín es buen oyente para los relatos que cuenta Molina en el tiempo libre. El libro cita muchas referencias a la psicología en sus notas al pie, pero no llega a distraer de la intensa amistad que se desarolla en la celda, un lugar de honestidad y generosidad.

En la celda, los dos prisioners se abren a la hone stidad. Valentín admite de no querer encariñarse con Molina, porque no quiere devolverle su geneorisadidad. Valentiín refiere a la "verguenza de los que no saben recibir, es porque tampoco les gusta dar nada". Un contraste interesante, es que Molina no termina de ser 100% honesto con Valentín, porque por un lado, da de comer a Valentín para que no se envene con la comida de cárcel, pero por otro lado busca sacar info de Valentín para poder ser liberado.

Entre los prisioneros se genera una generosidad natural, que funciona de manera que Molina cuente relatos, y Valentín busca que Molina se mantenga feliz. Molina se encariñe de Valentín y este cariño tambien se ve reflejado en Valentín cuando admite "vos sos la mumer araña, que atrapa a los hombres en su tela" (pg. 226). Valentín le ayuda a Molina desarollar auto-generosidad, con darse cuenta de que en algun momento, tiene que vivir su vida, o no la de su madre. Valentín le refuerza la idea de autovalorarse, cuando le dice de "prometer hacer que le respeten, osea no permitir que nadie le trate mal." Sin embargo, al querer ayudar a Valentín, Molina termina sacrificando su vida.

My Review:
[b:Haben: The Deafblind Woman Who Conquered Harvard Law|43211952|Haben The Deafblind Woman Who Conquered Harvard Law|Haben Girma|https://i.gr-assets.com/images/S/compressed.photo.goodreads.com/books/1548899016l/43211952._SY75_.jpg|67055143] is a riveting account of one woman's journey from girlhood to a promising career as a lawyer facing the obstacle of disability, by way of self-acceptance and pure passion for disability rights. I was impressed by Haben's sheer motivational drive to succeed, despite being invisible in many ableist contexts of school, work and play. I particularly enjoyed the story of Haben's trip to Mali, as it shows how despite the extreme context of being an "outsider" in a foreign country, Haben makes the most of her time and energy spent buidling schools in Mali.

One example of Haben's sheer motivational drive is how she is expected, as deafblind, to seek all her educational materials that other students are handed by default. Underneath a desire to just be a kid who is told what the homework is, is the crushing realization: " If I want to succeed, I’ll have to work to gain access to every visual detail and every spoken word. Every single time." (pg. 12). Not a moment can be spared when your default is exclusion from education. Uncomfortably, the reader realizes the burden is always on the disabled to get an education.

An interesting twist to Haben's work ethic is her realization that working hard is not the only requirement to prevent exclusion, but trusting in others to accept her. Haben recalls spending time with her family, in which they played a joke on her, and Haben working relentlessly to prove them wrong. "By focusing all my energy on proving my fearlessness, framing the situation as me-against-them, I perpetuated and guaranteed my own exclusion." (pg.38).

The story of Haben's biography is a series of short stories in which we learn on the one hand, just how unwelcoming a world constructed for the seeing and hearing is, and on the other hand, how far sheer motivation and passion can bring someone to achieving their wildest dreams. Haben dreamed about become a disability rights lawyer and is experiencing that reality today.

Title: The Lover's Dictionary
Author: David Levithan
My Review:
The Lover's Dictionary was released in 2011 and consists of a "dictionary-style" collection of short texts about love, such that each chapter reflects a new letter of the alphabet, with a corresponding word (and poem) starting with the letter of that alphabet. Because I had not read any kind of preface to the book, I was not aware that the book regards one particular couple's relationship over time; rather, I had believed each "dictionary" entry to be from a different couple.

The purpose of the author, therefore, is to show that every relationship has "ups" and "downs" and that disappointment, excitement, past and present all play an important role in the evolution of human romantic relationships. While I was hoping to see more entries regarding the positive side of love, I found the book to be more full of conflict than I expected.

My favorite entry in the book was "beware,v.", which told the story of a woman sharing her worst date experience. According to the woman, her date was so unpleasant that in order to get rid of the other person, she sticks out her tongue "like...a frog" when a fly appears at the table, and ends up catching it. The story embarasses the woman, and in the process shows vulnerability to the narrator of the book. This allowed an opportunity for another voice, other than the narrator's, to be understood and interpreted.

Title: Unpopular Essays
Author: Bertrand Russell
My Review:
Unpopular Essays is a book by Bertrand Russell published in 1950. Bertrand Russell is known for making contributions to epistemology (the theory of knowledge), and the philosophy of mathematics. To the general public, however, it is said that he was known as an anti-war campaigner and a writer on social and political issues. In the novel, Russell prevents his most controversial ideas. However, in 2019, these ideas regarding philosophy and politics have come to be generally accepted.

My favorite section regards the last chapter, "Ideas That Have Harmed Mankind". In this chapter, Russell refutes the notion that the male sex is the superior sex, saying that fallacy is a result of the sin of pride. Russel believes that "there was, I think, never any reason to believe in any innate superiority of the male, except his superior muscle. ... Male superiority in former days was easily demonstrated, because if a woman questioned her husband's he could beat her." In the past, having muscle power was most important to the enforcement of law, by way of militias or warlords. Russell mentions, however, that fortunately most modern nations have ruled out this notion.

The sin of pride is particularly interesting to consider byeond the text as it is almost a logical truth that most humans when referring to the "best" qualities, often think of their own qualities as the best. Who hasn't met a person who believes their country does the "best food", or has the "hardest language to learn"? Sometimes high-self esteem leads people to believe truths that are not universal.

Continuing this chapter, Russell also warns that "In America everybody is of opinion that he has no social superiors, since all men are equal, but he does not admit that he has no social inferiors, for, from the time of Jefferson onward, the doctrine that all men are equal applies only upwards, not downwards." This subject may have been controversial at the time, but there is no question that in 2019, rising economic equality is an issue. When we ask to be equal, are we making sure that also the people below us attain our quality of life? Perhaps thinking of our neighbors in this way will lead us to be less selfish and advance our economic causes together as a whole.

Title: Understanding the Borderline Mother: Helping Her Children Transcend the Intense, Unpredictable, and Volatile Relationship
Author: Christine Ann Lawson
My Review:
Understanding the Borderline Mother by Christine Ann Lawson is a deep insight into dysfunctional families presided over by a borderline mother and helps children of such mothers
recognize,  understand and accept their behavior. Lawson uses four categories of borderline mother to allow readers to easily identify their mother with a set of behaviors: the Waif, the Hermit, the Queen and the Witch. Furthermore, famous examples of such categories are given, such as  Princess Diana (Waif), Sylvia Plath (Hermit), Mary Todd Lincoln (Queen) and Joan Crawford (Witch). While the book clarifies that a mother will have a dominant state, the author is quick to clarify that in all types, children feel that expressing your own thoughts threatens the mother.

The Waif is said to be in the dominant state is helplessness, and lives by the message is that "Life is too hard". For someone who experiences a "waif" personality, accepting help is losing control, and helplessness is a defense against closeness and loss. The most revealing trait about this type is the reaction patients have had of trying to save their mother "I'm tired of trying to save her. I can barely save myself." This kind of borderline mother may even attracct a "Frog-prince" who is emotionally constricted and cannot understand emotional needs because his were unmet.

The Hermit mother is said to be in a dominant state of fear and lives by the message that "life is too dangerous". Someone who is a hermit mothers suffers from acute anxiety and expects to lose what they need. In the Hermit's case, "hermits and eating habits are bizarre" food serves to regulate anxiety and will self-soothe. Many "no-good" adult children may need to sever the relationship completely in cases of ongoing denigration. The most constructive method to make in reply to a hermit are "I am" statements, because borderlines lack of object constancy, they have no access to an internal self that is constant and are not capable of recognizing the needs in their children. They may seek a husband that is a "huntsman" who fulfills his duty to his conscience and defines his self-worth to the extent his behavior matches his principles.

The Queen mother is entitled to invade the boundaries of others and take what she needs, has a dominant state of emptiness, and lives by the motto that "life is about me". Those who are Queens have no memory of being special and devalues those who do not provide special treatment. Among strategies given tr felt shame foo cope with the Queen are "Say no with your actions, not just with words," and "be wary of gifts with strings attached." I found these tips extremely helpful in dealing with my own mother as I have shame for just existing, having needs and having a self. This kind of mother may choose a husband that is a "King", who together with the Queen creates a shared delusion of happiness, requiring constant attention and admiration. Interestingly, the Witch wiithin the Queen may emerge when others fail to admire her.

Finally, the last type discussed is the Witch, which is described as the most harmful to a child, where the dominant state is annihilating rage and the message is "Life is War". At any moment, a borderline mother may turn into this stage, which is one of life-threatening rejection. Children of borderlines may not remember details of attack, but are extremely sensitive to indication of imminent attacks. Typically the Witch is capable of organizing a campaign of denigration, stirs up conflict in groups and violates the boundaries of others out of fear of entrapment. The Witch may seek out a "Fisherman", a man who typically were either motherless or had sadistic and controlling mothers. They may have never known healthy love and mistake aggression for courage. Unfortunately, this kind of man will often relinquish his will to the Witch.

While there are many types of borderline  mothers, this book is particularly useful for adult children who can decide the direction their relationship wants to take, whether it be acceptance, coping or distance-making. The patient is told that being oneself does not solve problems, but it does free one to explore new solutions, consider new perspectives and experience greater intmiacy. In the case of conflict, respond to domination (the imposition of one's will on another) with firmness, the expression of the conviction of one's own will. Someone who is declining to hear 'no' is a signal that they are seeking control. At the end of the day, it is the responsibility of those who understand the condition to be a beacon to those still caught in a life lived backwards due to the stresses of co-living with someone with this condition.

Title: A Random Walk Down Wall Street: The Time-Tested Strategy for Successful Investing
Author: Burton G. Malkiel
My Review:
A Random Walk Down Wall Street is a book by author Burton Malkiel, an economist who spent 28 years as the director of the Vanguard Group. Malkiel is a strong proponent of the efficient market hypothesis, the idea that markets that allow for free flow of information will stabilize to reflect the most recent information, limiting the opportunities for arbitrage. In financial economics, arbitrage is the act of profiting from a difference in market prices. Overall, Malkiel believes that the market usually reflects the most recent information, and that to "beat the market", one should invest in index funds.

Regarding his other techniques, Malkiel notes that when using technical analysis and fundamental analysis, both have their flaws, and that passive strategies will often pay more in the long-run due to the high fees associated with frequent trading. Regarding actively managed mutual funds, he cites examples of funds having good past performance under performing in later periods, regressing towards a mean that will not outperform other indices.

The most useful bit of information was the knowledge that diversifying your profile to include international assets can have a big pay-off, as well as investing in smaller stocks. Malkiel states "...investors can reduce risk by diversifying internationally, by including asset classes such as real estate in the portfolio, and by placing some portion fo their portfolio in bonds." In addition he informs us that "although the smaller stocks were riskier than the major blue-chips... a well - diversified portfolio of small companies is likely to produce significantly enhanced returns."

Some other interesting techniques mentioned are: treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), dollar-cost averaging, and investing in art objects and collectibles. Malkiel informs that TIPS are not ideal for taxable investors, and best used in tax-advantaged retirement plans. Regarding investment in collectibles, he states that "the inflation adjusted value of art objects and collectibles does not generally increase" and to earn money collecting,"you need great originality and taste."

Title: Between the World and Me
Author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
My Review:
Between the World and Me, written by Ta-Nehisi Coates (Tah-Nuh-Hah-See KOHTS) is stylized to be read as a letter written from father to son in the same vein as James Baldwin´s essay "My Dungeon Shook — Letter to my Nephew on the One Hundredth Anniversary of Emancipation".

I found this book after reading his piece for the Atlantic "The Case for Reparations" that won a George Polk award. This is an author who truly shows a fearlessness for direct conversation. It is clear that Mr. Coates also doesn't settle for the first answers he finds in his life, nor in his writing. The main idea he expresses in this short story is that "blackness" comes with an entire history of brutality forced upon a group of people that can´t be erased, but with a heritage of diversity that deserves to be celebrated.

The idea that a group of people who self-identify as white, or rather, not black, continue to accept destruction of minority groups as a way towards self-promotion can be hard to hear, especially if you are a young person that believes the world is more equal than ever before. However, by reviewing Ta-Nehisi's personal history of racist experiences from childhood through adulthood, it is clear that at least in his world there existed people who have harmed "black bodies" without a second thought.

Title: The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress
Author: Robert A. Heinlein
My Review:
The Moon is a Harsh Mistress is a sci-fi novel written by Robert A. Heinlen and published in 1966. The story, taking place in 2075, is told form the point of view of a computer technician, Mannie (Manuel Garcia O’ Kelly), living on the moon. Under a “Lunar Authority”, the lunar denizens we come across quickly hatch a plan to become their own nation.

While reading the story, the reader can relate questions of artificial intelligence, human rights, and economic liberty to today’s setting, 2017. How does a nation go about claiming independence (as Kurdish people in Syria, Turkey are asking)? What happens when a middle class feels insecure about their material well-being (as a rising middle class in China is discovering)? How comfortable are we with technology disrupting our lives?

The philosophical questions that Heinlen lays before us make us inspired to double-check the structures our society have come to accept as unchangeable, and question them in favor of something better, or at least, something different. And as the first book to introduce me to “There Ain’t No Such Thing as a Free Lunch” (TANSTAAFL), I’m grateful to say that I can look at everyday decisions, and see them with the long-term in mind.

While this book was a challenge to complete (due to a lot of invented lingo), the experience made me feel better prepared for today's intellectual debates. I would be interested to see how other classic sci-fi has been influenced by Heinlein's work.

Title: Roadside Picnic
Author: Arkady Strugatsky
Additional Authors: Boris Strugatsky, Theodore Sturgeon, Antonina W. Bouis
My Review:
This book was sufficiently creepy and overall I loved it. I discovered this book when they referenced it on The Black Tapes podcast with Alex Reagan. The introduction and the buildup slowed me down with a lot of details, but the action-y bits and the climax/end are worth waiting for.

This book comes with a lot of lingo that'd you'd associate with Anthony Burgess and "nadstat" his fictional language used in A Clockwork Orange. Some of the invented words in this book include:

"the visitation"->referring to the period of time in which unidentified objects were first scattered
"the zone"-> the region where unidentified objects have been found
"empty"-> a canister with two discs and blue liquid in between
"greenhorn"-> a newbie
"stalker"->one who enters the zone hoping to capture empties

All of the characters are fairly interesting and the book is set up as third person (limited omniscient), so that we see everything that happens, but through a character's bias.
Although too many characters might be confusing to the reader (as when a person describes a friend of a friend), some of the best details add to the creepiness. For example, we find out that children born to those who visit the zone grow up with mutations; plus, the people who have found special objects in the zone don't know how they got there!

If you don't worry about remembering all the characters, this book will feel like a five star story.

My Review: The Soul of an Octopus by Sy Montgomery is about the intelligent qualities that the octopus shows in captivity. In particular, the book describes the bonds that Montgomery (naturalist but not scientist) with the animals in the New England Aquarium in Boston, MA, starting with an octopus called Athena in 2011. After reading the book, I am certain that the octopus, despite being part of the mollusk family (a family to which snails, slugs, clams and oysters also belong) is highly intelligent to human convention. However, I found that the book normalized too much the practice of capturing wild animals to fill an aquarium, for the purpose of teaching. In fact, the most rewarding aspect of the book was seeing how Sy Montgomery bonded with other volunteers at the aquarium, rather than the animals.

Title: A Death in Belmont
Author: Sebastian Junger
My Review:
A Death in Belmont is an investigative look into a series of murders that occurred in Boston in the early 1960s. The genre of the book is true crime, as Sebastian Junger is retelling his investigation into the judicial process that brought a man named Roy Smith in a suspect for the murder of Bessie Goldberg, a crime for which he ultimately gets convicted. Ultimately, the main theme of the book is the inability to extract certainty in an uncertain world, and the resulting injustice that is produced when we rely on our instincts (or prejudices) to answer questions of mortal importance. The main theme is that, at least historically, depending on the color of your skin you may be more likely "assumed guilty until proven innocent".

The most shocking example of racism is how Roy Smith is convicted of the crime based on the details of time and money given by the accused himself, rather than hard evidence found in the apartment. Furthermore is the fact that Roy Smith is recorded as undergoing a nearly 12-hour interrogation, enough time for anyone to become stressed to the point of admitting to crimes they did not commit for the sake of "putting" and end to it. Some details point to the fact that despite his criminal background, Roy Smith never fled nor admitted to having committed the crime. He likely had faith that one day, his truth would be revealed.

On a positive note, the book takes notice of positive changes in the law, such as prison reform on page 209: "If a man is returned to society more embittered, vengeful, demoralized and incapable of social and economic survival than when he first came to prison, then we certainly ... have failed to protect society". Noticeable achievements of Roy while in prison, such as taking college-level courses while having only continued school into eighth grade, was one detail that contributes to the argument of Roy's innocence.

If you like police dramas and can handle gruesome details, this book is likely for you. I would have enjoyed a third person perspective, as ultimately the book reads like a biography of the author's time spent as a reporter, almost certainly not taking as much as a stance on comments like "All DeSalvo's rapes, Dr. Robey believed, were actually seductions, and the supposed rape victims had simply regretted their decision afterward and called the police." (pg. 227). A stronger opinion on outdated comments would sit well with more modern-minded readers.

Title: The Bell Jar
Author: Sylvia Plath
My Review:
The Bell Jar by Sylvia Plath is considered a staple American feminist novel, where a college-aged Esther Greenwood, confronts issue of identity and mental illness after taking a summer internship with a prominent NYC magazine. Sylvia actually published this book under the name Victoria Lucas out of her desire to spare the feelings of her mother and previous boyfriend Dick Norton. Hence, this novel is considered a roman-a-clef, in French literally "a novel with a key", such that events and people are understood to be real, but appear with invented names.

As is, this novel is very unique, in the way the reader sees a direct stream of consciousness style of writing when Esther faces varios comedic incidents kicked off by a banquet held by the Ladies' Day magazine. However, calling this writing the "female equivalent" of J.D. Salinger would be wrong, as Plath explores her identity through a uniquely female perspective, focusing on the pressures that society places on her for being a woman.

The conflict that Esther as a woman faces in New york, is in deciding who she wants to be, either a pious "good girl", or a sarcastic "rebel". This reflected in the friends she spends time with in NYC. While she spends most of her time with Doreen, she also acknowledges that she could never be as free as Doreen. However, we do see her admire the goodness of Betsy, who always does the right thing.

After leaving New York, we also see conflict in Esther wanting to be a published writer, but sometimes feeling hopeless, and not minding life as a matronly women. We see her fantasize a standard life with a husband (represented by the hypocritical Buddy Willard) or with a large amount of children, like Dodo Conway, Esther's fertile neighbor with six children.

Finally, in her first hospitalization for mental illness, we see Esther struggle to have her own opinions and control of her body when visiting Doctor Gordon. In her visits, Doctor Gordon appears to be self-interested, easily dismissing Esther's case, and immediately subjecting her to therapy as a form of punishment, for not fitting into "society's standards" of a woman.

I appreciate this novel for its honesty. It was painful to read Esther's struggles knowing that patriarchal society was a major cause for her heightened suffering. Every incident that occurs somehow seems to be aggravated because Esther is a woman. Some of the most frustrating, but honest moments, are when Esther sees women putting down other women, as when she tries to bring flowers to the maternity ward, but is judged by those mothers for "mixing the flowers", or when her mother thinks that Esther's illness is somehow some failure of her own, to not raise her daughter correctly.

However, I am not interested in re-reading this novel, as I know that while it provides a snapshot of Sylvia's life in 1953, New York City, I know that American society has changed enough for this novel to feel recent; but it is worth noting that with fourth-wave feminism and the Time's Up Movement, some readers may decide that patriarchy and sexual harassment is very much still around.

Title: Just Kids
Author: Patti Smith
My Review:
Just Kids is a memoir published in 2010 in honor of the friendship artist Patti Smith shared with her best friend and ex-lover Robert Mapplethorpe. Being a memoir, the novel covers the period of time from when Patti Smith first arrived to New York in 1967, to the time of her marriage with Fred "Sonic" Smith in 1980's, when she moved to Michigan.

The main argument of the book was that Patti Smith had a passion for all kind of art, having dabbled in trinket-making, poetry, theatre, and then song-writing and singing, but was never recognized for her art until she was promoted by the inner circle of artists that her partner Robert Mapplethorpe obtained.

Patti was living in New York at the height of the Hippie Movement from the 60's and 70's as well as the punk rock scene, having frequented Max's Kansas City and CBGB. The book struck me as incredibly informative of the counterculture of the 1960s and the punk rock of the 70's in New York. I was introduced to several artists I had never heard of before this book such as Loulou de la Falaise, Brian Jones, John McKendry and Maxime de la Falaise.

The most remarkable source of inspiration for Patti Smith was [a:Arthur Rimbaud|72605|Arthur Rimbaud|https://images.gr-assets.com/authors/1418930475p2/72605.jpg], having said to have first found his work in a Philadelphia bus depot, as a 99 cent paperback. In direct contrast to Patti's poetic style was Robert's style, who felt the need to participate in his extreme art, such as making the public more aware of the practice of S&M. He felt he was in a privileged position, so he documented this niche area as art.

The he book most engaging part of the book was Patti's descriptions of her outings with Robert, before and after being lovers. She describes "strolls on Myrtle Ave., searching for Mallomars", as well as travelling to Coney Island. During her visits to Max's Kansas City, she describes not feeling attached to Andy Warhol's central table, but feeling finally accepted when Robert and her receive the invitation.

The most shocking move was finding Patti's move from poetry to song-writing and singing. Somehow, without explanation, and through the connections she had with artists through Robert, she was able to record her first song at Electric Lady with her label "Mer", and then her first album "Horses" with Arista Records. After her recordings, she was able to play regularly as a band at CBGB, splitting the bill with Television.

Besides observing how Patti received eventual recognition the artists around her, the book doesn't prove that her art was exceptional in itself, but rather that Patti was able to elevate her art thanks to the promotion by influential others.

Title: The Lady with the Little Dog
Author: Anton Chekhov
My Review:
"The Lady with the Little Dog" is a short story written by Anton Chekhov published in 1899. The title immediately implies that woman mentioned will be mysterious. Indeed, the implication is correct - the story is about Anna Sergeyevna, a woman who is unhappily married and chooses to vacation in Yalta alone. A man named Dmitri Gurov, easily capable of seducing women, is intrigued by Anna, and proceeds to have an affair with her.

The sections of the book are broken into a) meeting in Yalta, b) the affair in Yalta, c) Gurov seeking the presence of Anna at her home in St. Petersburg and d) Anna's visits to Moscow. The amazing aspect of this story is that both characters, in their middle age, actually fall in love.

The conflict in the story comes from the issue of faithfulness - both characters fake "happiness" in their day-to-day lives, but in secret aspire for a true, passionate relationship. When both characters become determined to commit to their relationship, we learn that the moral of the story is that any affair has a high probability of failure, as turning something playful into something real is the "hardest part".

Title: Juliet Takes a Breath
Author: Gabby Rivera
My Review:
Juliet Takes a Breath covers the story of Juliet Milagros Palante, a young, hispanic teenager who makes the move to Portland in order to complete an internship with her feminist idol " Harlowe Brisbane ". The book chronologically follows Juliet's already-made realization of being gay and having a white girlfriend, to making several discoveries about racism that can exist even within gay communities. The novel is effective as a coming-of-age and allows for empathy to build for anyone that identifies as a woman, a gay person, or a minority.

From Juliet's point of view, we see that Juliet understands the importance of her mom and her Puerto Rican family, but at the same time is true to herself, by acknowledging her attraction to woman, even hanging up on her mom when she says that liking girls is "just a phase".

When Juliet meets Harlowe, the reader learns some nice tips from this character of Harlow, like how to wash out blood from clothing, and how to connect with my own body when in pain. However, when Harlowe shows discrete racism by saying Juliet was just a survivor of the shot-up Bronx, facing the character of Harlowe was rather uncomfortable.

This book changed my view of traditional Puerto Rican households. While I would have thought that these families were cruel for not accepting homosexuality, I realized that every household has a certain amount of love, and in Juliet's case, she gets a lot of love from her family. The character of Lil' Melvin being gay was an interesting detail for Juliet to get to play a mentor too. The relationship of Juliet with her family shows that as long as you are honest, family will love you anyways!

Despite being uplifting, I wish that the author wouldn't include so much talk of weed in this novel. It feels like marijuana is being worshiped for curing ailments, and bringing people together for Juliet, which I don't think is super appropriate, given this is a teen novel!

Title: The Left Hand of Darkness
Author: Ursula K. Le Guin
My Review:
The Left Hand of Darkness written by Ursula K. Le Guin and published in 1969. In the novel, a young explorer called Genly Ai arrives at the planet Gethen, hoping to bring the population into the inter-planetary alliance called the Ekumen. In this cross-planet alliance, technology and ideas are shared, but there is no external government, but rather "communal cooperation". There are no laws, but rather ideas that get implemented when a voting board arrives at a consensus. Throughout the book, Ursula Le Guin tells the story through the transformation of Genly as the archetypal male-centric science fiction reader, and argues for the inclusion of fluid-gender thinking, as an extension of Taoism.

Throughout the novel, Genly shows signs of being arrogant towards "female qualities". When he meets Estraven, he describes not trusting his "charm" and describes any show of playfulness as sly or "otter-like". While Estraven completely trusts Genly and puts his life in danger for the sake of Genly's mission, Genly admits to never fully being able to trust Genly because he cannot place his sexuality or understand his motives. Fortunately, towards the end, he finally appreciates Estraven for who he is:“I saw then again … what I had always been afraid to see, and had pretended not to see in [Estraven]: that he was a woman as well as a man”.

The "wholeness" of being man and woman reflects Le Guin's believe in Taoism. According this philosophy of Chinese origin, life should be lived with balance and virtue. It is clear that Le Guin has studied this philosophy, for when she allows Genly to love Estraven, she teaches the reader to value each person as a "man" and "woman". This is probably every "feminist's" dream, as every woman probably wants to feel like a human, first, and a woman, second. When Estraven makes his choice to not continue in the end, it also reflects that in Taoism, we are eternal, and we with the Tao in life and in death.

This book was mind-opening on a very individual, personal and spiritual level. I would have never expected Le Guin to combine feminist ideas with religous ones, to come together in a story so revolutionary, and that holds up to time. I hold her in high respect to being able to explore feminist ideas from a cisgender male, who often is considered the archetypal science fiction reader. I think that being a woman made Le Guin create a more flexible main character, one who was able to grow fond of a friend who was non-traditional, and thus become a better person by the end of the book.

Title: Black Box
Author: Jennifer Egan
My Review:
Jennifer Egan is a Pulitzer-prize winning author that has written pieces in non-traditional ways, employing techniques like second-person narrative and implementing post-modern writing (using fragmentation, for example, to change the order of events). Black Box is a short story written by Jennifer Egan in the form of a series of tweets released on The New Yorker's Twitter account in May of 2012. The book takes place at some time in the future, when technology has allowed American spies, particularly women, to complete tasks with built-in bodily devices.

The main idea of the book is that an unnamed woman, working as a volunteer spy, has to overcome challenges at her job that question her dignity but overall reflect her patriotism. Due to the grey area of morality in the novel, and the use of second-person narrative, the story feels like it is happening in real time.

During this novel, there are times when the reader will be in real pain, knowing that the woman has to make difficult decisions, such as being unfaithful to her husband, in order to make a useful contact with a terrorist. Other times, the reader will probably be excited for the intelligence of this woman, knowing that if she uses her surroundings properly, she can escape.

The best part of this short story is the technology described: a microphone behind your right ear canal, the data plug between the fourth and pinky toe for data gathering. This is an interesting adventure story and the briefness of the plot makes the story thrilling.
