Title: The Whisperer in Darkness
Author: H.P. Lovecraft
My Review:
One of the most frightful things about scientific investigation is fear of retribution for your findings. In "The Whisperer in Darkness" the narrator and folklorist Albert Wilmarth embarks on a exploration of "creatures" recently seen in the hills of Virginia after flooding in 1927. As Albert becomes more involved in the controversy, he gets a letter from a Henry Wentworth Akeley, who claims to have proof of the existence of the alien race.

In this novel, H.P. Lovecraft captures the narrator's curiosity and turns it into an element of danger. Albert's total willingness to meet with Mr. Akeley after a sudden change of tone in their letters of exchange represents total foolishness. The reader can already conclude that Mr. Akeley was probably kidnapped, and yet Albert's curiosity must be satisifed.

When he goes to visit Akeley's house, he finds that all farm animals are missing, and that Akeley has been ill and has remained immobile in a chair in the corner. Upon waking the next morning, and discovering face and hands in Akeley's chair, Albert flees the house.

While the major fear in the story is if the alien-creatures will attempt harm Albert, a greater fear is that of a race which has appeared to master machinery, time-travel and flight. While readers might assume that Henry left willingly, it is hard to be sure, and we are left not knowing whether to like or despise the creatures.

The lack of clear answers about the alien race was intriguing but frustrating. One is left wondering what really happened to Akeley, and if in his own pursuits he was destroyed, or elevated to a higher plane of knowledge.

Title: Carry On (Simon Snow, #1)
Author: Rainbow Rowell
My Review:
Carry On is a book written by Rainbow Rowell about the last year at Watford School of Magicks for Simon Snow, a magical student who is based off of a fan fiction character from Rowell's earlier 2013 novel Fangirl. During the novel, Simon confronts his prophesy of defeating The Humdrum, the antagonist of the story who steals magic from the atmosphere such that wizards cannot use their magic in these "dead spots". During his last year of school he faces off with his hostile roommate Baz, while spending time with his disinterested girlfriend Agatha and his closest friend Penelope (Penny).

The book is thrilling to anyone who misses the Harry Potter universe, but the slight differences between this world and the Harry Potter world can be clashing, such as comparing The Mage and Dumbledore, and make you realize that Rowell's creation is completely different from Rowling's creation.

The most creative aspect of this book was the world-building that happens for the way magic works. Spells in the book are said to be common phrases from Normals (the people without magic) and that the more used a phrase (whether stated or written), the more power it has. For example, Simon says “Penny falls asleep in the middle of telling me about a song she’s heard, a song she thinks will be a spell someday, though I can’t think of any use for Call Me Maybe”. The fact that words hold so much power in this universe is very appealing to avid readers.

The biggest motif is the idea that magic should be accessible to all, not just one social class. Natasha Grimm-Pitch, Baz's mother and the former headmistress of Watford, was said to only let students in with the purist magic. When The Mage implements reforms, he succeeds in opening Watford to every child “blessed with magic”, but was over zealous in his desire to become powerful himself, such as arranging his placement as Headmaster. Powerful families of the Council are concerned with preserving their families magic as it is believed that magic can be diluted over time.

This book is surely to warn young people of the danger in being over zealous, and the challenges and remind older readers the joy of the Harry Potter world, and relying on your friends to survive the trials of adulthood.

Title: Un cementerio perfecto
Author: Federico Falco
My Review:
Federico Falco es un narrador cordobés de General Cabrera. El publicó su libro Un Cementerio perfecto en 2016 que consiste de varios relatos. El ha dicho en una entrevista que no le interesa ser un escritor que genere comodidad, y definitivamente cada cuento como "Las liebres", "Silvi y la Noche Oscura", "Un cementerio perfecto", "La actividad forestal" y "El río" hace al lector un poco incomodo aunque le hace pensar sobre la realidad de la gente.

A veces sentí que algunos cuentos comentaban tantas observaciones sobre la gente en general que no sabia a veces cual era el propósito de haberlos contado. Por ejemplo en "Las liebres" sentí que no hubo tanto conflicto con respecto a la vida de la persona en la cueva del monte, solitaria pero en contacto a veces con su viejo pueblo. Después, en "La actividad forestal" parecía que hubiera sentido tragedia Mabel por lo que pasó con su padre, y por su casamiento a un desconocido, pero el lector se entiende que la vida de Mabel es así y que durante toda la trama ella ya lo había aceptado eso.

Sin embargo, la creatividad y a veces la fantasía con que el autor inventa cada lugar hace irresistible el libro. Muchas decisiones tomadas por los personajes son discutibles y por lo tanto me hacen querer compartir el libro para ver que opinarían mis amigos sobre estas acciones. Es imposible dejar de leer cada cuento y incluso me quedé identificando con algunos personajes.

Title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, Parts 1 & 2
Author: John Tiffany
My Review:
Given that this was a play I only read, and did not see, the following review approaches the work by analyzing the play as a written piece.

I was not able to see this play in person because I do not live anywhere near London. As the official eigth Harry Potter Story, one could easily give the play 5 stars, just for fulfilling one's morbid curiousity about what happened to Harry Potter's after the epilogue in Book 7. This script, officially credited to Jack Thorne, is fulfilling; however, by attempting to develop the childrens' characters of the story as much as the adults' characters, both parties can feel under-developed.

In the play, we encounter Albus Severus Potter, Harry's middle child and next to enter Hogwarts struggling with his identity. As a typical adolescent, he rejects his father's expectations while at the same trying to gain his approval. When the opportunity strikes, we see that Albus forms a bond with another outcast, and makes a team with a stranger to try to change the world in a way that will make his name famous on its own.

What's unusual about this play is that we get to see a side of Harry as a father, and all his weaknesses when it comes to being the dad he never had. I recommend this play entirely; being taken on a trip that revists many scenes of the previous books is pure adrenaline. However, if you're looking for the classic motifs, and the classic players of the story - none of that is here. The trio of Ron, Hermione and Harry, now parents, have lost some dynamic they had as children, to be replaced with the dynamic of their children. Additionally, the themes of loyalty in the novels, have been replaced with mistrust here - with Albus' mistrust of family, with his new need to make alliances in a way that forges himself a new identity.

Regardless of any thoughts, the play is important enough as a sequel to the series that it is paramount of any reader to complete it - just expect big changes to the universe, and lots of them!

Title: Pachinko
Author: Min Jin Lee
My Review:
Pachinko released in 2017 by Min Jin Lee, follows four generations of a Korean family that moves to Japan before WWII, experiencing life there all the way until the 1980's. The story is a tale of love and accumulation of wealth among many generations. The slow development of the first two generations stories leads to quick development of the next two Japanese born generations, providing an interesting contrast of tradition with rule-breaking as well as subordination with rebellious spirit.

The story initially follows a young girl named Sunja who has an extramarital affair with a wealthy trader named Koh Hansu. Ashamed of the affair, Sunja ends up marrying Baek Isak, a Presbyterian minister who as a favor to Sunja's mother for nursing him out of sickness and to god, promises to care for Sunja.

The main motifs are loyalty: staying loyal to family is reflected again as Yangjin refuses to reject her husband just for his disability, as Sunja promises to be loyal to Isak. Another motif is that of discrimination against hte Korean characters: of Japanese thinking of Koreans as lazy or complaining, of businessmen regarding "pachinko" business owners as gangsters, of the assumption that most koreans thus work in "pachinko" because of some kind of inherit sinfulness.

As Sunja manages to raise her family in Osaka, where Baek Isak moved the family, she discovers that church leaders have been imprisoned for assumed insubordinance to the Japanese emperor. Despite having Noa born as Hansu's true son, she raises him and son to Isak, Mozasu, as children to Isak. She maintains Hansu's existence as a secret, with the family assuming some man had taken advantage of her before in Korea.

As WWII advances and threatens to spill into Japanese borders, Sunja realizes Koh Hansu never really abandonded her and had ensured jobs for her and her sister-in-law making kimchi in a restaurant during the war. The progression of Noa and Mozasu's lives then take drastic turns. Noa, upon learning of his true Korean "gangster/trader" origins, rejects his family entirely and leaves the prestigious Waseda university. Mozasu, never having appreciated school, becomes a master at the pachinko "pinball" business.

This book is a good representation of the challenges of growing up as an immigrant in a foreign country.

Title: Logic: The Ancient Art of Reason (Wooden Books)
Author: Earl Fontainelle
My Review:
Logic first published in 2016, provides a neat summary of practical logic and reasoning. According to this book, logic is considered the foundation of the three linguistic arts of logic, grammar, and rhetoric. Reason engages us with the present, by helping us understand the past and plan for the future, while logic is said to be the laws by which reason operates.

After the introduction, this book is divided into about 30 sub-sections, each which describe a different component of logic. While most sections cover topics that a high school class in English writing will teach you, some sections were surprisingly refreshing such as: 1) dilemmas and 2) linguistic/non linguistic fallacies.

The most useful section I read from this book was dealing with dilemmas. According to this book dilemmas can be dealt with in two ways. First, is grasping the horns of a dilemma. With such a method, you show that one or both of the major premises is false. This will break the connection between the antecedent and the consequent. Second, dilemmas can be met with a counter dilemma, with rebuttal. This is done by constructing a new dilemma from the same premises, but with a new and opposite conclusion.

My favorite section overall in its surprising conclusions was the existence of linguistic and non-linguistic fallacies. In linguistic fallacies, one can take distributive qualities and attribute them to the collective (composition fallacy) or then can take collective qualities and attribute them to distributive ones (division fallacy). Regarding non-linguistic fallacies, some include the "in this respect" (what is true in certain respects is assumed true in all respects), "during this, therefore because of this" (where because two things occur at the same time, they must be linked), and finally "complex question fallacy" (smuggling an assumption into the question and demanding a single answer).

Title: The Sympathizer (The Sympathizer, #1)
Author: Viet Thanh Nguyen
My Review:
The Sympathizer was written by Vietnamese American author Viet Thanh Nguyen, who in 1975, fled with his family to the United States after the Fall of Saigon. The theme of this book is one of “tangledness”. The unnamed narrator is a half-French and half-Vietnamese young man who is a communist double agent, confessing to his communist captors. The narrator completed college in the US, but was raised in Vietnam, and faces his mixed identity when it becomes tangled with experiences of growing up as a "foreigner" in his homeland. He finds himself in situations that increasingly question his loyalty to the Communist cause, his friends and his lovers as he works as a spy against the Special Branch in America, the central intelligence organization of the anti-Communist South Vietnamese Army.

This was Viet Thanh Nguyen's debut novel, published in 2015 and had wild success as a best-seller and having won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, as well as seven other awards! What is truly remarkable about this novel is that it is told from the perspective of a conflicted subversive and idealist working as a double agent. I would have expected that a Communist narrator would have rubbed many readers the wrong way. If the novel has offended any Americans, I haven't found out, because many readers talk about the novel being eye-opening to them!

This novel uses satire of the American military, Hollywood, and American customs to point out that while America feels it is the "winner", just like any country, it has made many political mistakes, hurting many people in the process. The war in Vietnam may have been many things - call it whatever you want (targeted action, campaign, or counter-terrorism) but it was technically wasn't a war that was declared by Congress. The last time the US Congress formally declared war on any nation was in 1942, was when war was declared against the Axis powers of Bulgaria, Hungary and Romania. After Congress repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution in January 1971 and President Richard Nixon continued to wage war in Vietnam, Congress passed the War Powers Resolution (Pub.L. 93–148), actually attempting to rein in some of the president's claimed powers.

Some of my favorite satire was to point out the hypocrisy of military leaders. In describing the discontent of the General (working as part of the South Vietnamese army) trying to live in the US. "The General merely a figurehead who occasionally bellowed at his children like one of those dusty lions in the zoo undergoing a midlife crisis" - pg. 79.The quote shows the fatigue of a once well-respected military leader living as a refugee in the US. 

Other quotes are particularly harsh on American liberties, such as this reference to the Declaration of Independence:
"Now a guarantee of happiness - that's a great deal. But a guarantee to be allowed the jackpot of happiness? Merely an opportunity to buy a lottery ticket. Someone would surely win millions, but millions would surely pay for it."- pg. 187.
While it is a harsh critique on a fundamental right, these words point out the practicality of the application of the right, in a world where economic inequalities become multiplied over generations.

Another quote critiques the American Dream, arguing that the American Dream is more for already-Americans than it is for immigrants:
"It's refugee numbers were hobbled by their structural function in the American Dream, which was to be so unhappy as to make other Americans grateful for their unhappiness" - pg. 187.

Overall, the narrator shows resilience an comitment to his friends in the book. Because the narrator is considered a "bastard", he learns that with school, he could be "twice as good" as everyone else. He relies on his smarts, and thinking of every problem in his life as an "exam to pass" in order to get himself out of difficult situations. The narrator shows us a more complex view of the Vietnamese refugee than some people are comfortable with - that although some Vietnamese people might have been considered anti-American during the war, more than anything, they are just 100% Vietnamese.

Title: Bad Feminist
Author: Roxane Gay
My Review:
Bad Feminist is a collection of essays released in 2014 by author Roxane Gay. The book is divided into sections called Me; Gender & Sexuality; Race & Entertainment; Politics, Gender & Race; and Back to Me. Overall, I was hoping to receive a bittersweet memoir about how she became a feminist; however, throughout the novel frustration placed against specific lived experiences leads me to believe that her anger is misdirected and that her definition of feminism is based on a negative definition. Unfortunately, it is easier to contrast something with what it isn't than define exactly what it is. In addition, when Gay mentions media criticism of TV shows, books, or music, she does not use these examples to further support a larger argument of feminism, rather they just stand as complaints.

Some of the most interesting discussions that occur are when Gay comments on the intersection of women and race. When talking about Tyler Perry's movie success. In Gay's blog it is cited that "The problem is that Tyler Perry is building his success on the backs of black women and the working class, by using them, all too often, to teach his lessons, to make his points, or to make them the butts of his jokes. In many of Perry’s movie, women are not to be trusted." After seeing Tyler Perry movies, I can only agree that Perry provides a simplified version of the "female", especially when trying to prove that a woman deserved punishment by acting immorally. Gay has very insightful commentary regarding how the black community might accept Perry's movies, because they fill a huge vacuum of black entertainment that is not being offered in modern cinema.

Unfortunately, some of the more frustrating passages involve Gay's childhood sexual abuse, which appear to come up in different chapters and not in a chronological order. I think that it is important to understand Gay's background of abuse to understand her perspective as an author, but perhaps more time would have been needed to ease the reader into what is a truly horrific tale of traumatic abuse.

Title: China Dolls
Author: Lisa See
My Review:
China Dolls is a 2014 novel about the world of Chinese nightclubs in the U.S. in the 1930's before the U.S. goes to war with Japan. The book is organized into three sections based on the opening quote "Only three things cannot be long hidden: the sun, the moon, and the truth." (Buddha). The first section is the Sun (October 1938 to July 1940), the second the Moon (August 1940-September 1945) and the third the Truth (December 1945 - June 1948). The central message to China Dolls is that resilience overcomes adversity. However, some of the characters themselves felt unreal, like caricatures of historical figures.

In the beginning of the book, we meet Grace, Helen and Ruby, three women who meet by chance when auditioning for the Forbidden City nightclub in San Francisco. Grace Lee is an American-born Chinese girl escaping her hometown, Helen lives with her traditional and proud family, and Ruby Tom is a defiant and ambitious dancer. Each of the girls carries their own secrets, which are not revealed until later, and threaten the very stability of their friendship. However, their resilience and reliance on each other allows them to overcome personal betrayals and the struggles of living in the wartime.

The best part about this novel is the research See conducted and used to inspire her characters in China Dolls . The interviews with real people, Michael Ching (son of the so-labeled the Chinese Frank Sinatra), Trudi Long, a performer (sponsored by Lee Mortimer after being interned), and Dorothy Toy (labeled the Chinese Ginger Rogers) particularly helped see to capture the details fo the Chinese-American nightclub scene.

Unfortunately, due to it's very historically-based writing, some of the characters do not feel complex. For example, while the story alternates between the different girls' perspectives, we see that Helen often quotes Chinese proverbs, which feels too gimmicky, given that we already know she was raised in a traditional way. “Every bush and tree looks like the enemy,” Helen says, using one of the many Chinese proverbs she often spouts, and Ruby, who is hiding her true ethnicity, feels she “was not only dancing on the edge of a volcano, she was looking down into its fiery center.” Later we find out that Helen has suffered a traumatic experience when she was younger, but reciting proverbs to support her dialogue feels hacky.

Title: Rebecca
Author: Daphne du Maurier
My Review:
Daphne du Maurier, an English author, first published Rebecca in 1938. The novel follows the retelling by the narrator of her experience marrying the heir of an English estate, called Maxim de Winter. Du Marnier is known for her narrative craft and her moody tones and inclusion of the paranormal. This novel reflects an intriguing horror story, with a structure of the tragedy occurring first, then the preceding actions and the mystery revealed at the end.

I came into this book with a recommendation by Our Shared Shelf on Goodreads, and was expecting moral questions or underlying themes of feminism to be explored. Instead, I believe the book to have provided more entertainment factor, than any intellectual questioning, and for that I found it dry. As a story, I would have preferred to see it in some other format, like film.

The story of Rebecca is highly romanticized and I believe undervalues women as complex characters. While I appreciated that the author was female, I was surprised to see such one-dimensional female characters. The narrator herself, the second Mrs. de Winter, never actually gets a name, and by being dim-witted, doesn't really spark me as a charismatic narrator. The older Mr. Winter I almost feel puts her down when he proposes marriage: "No, I'm asking you to marry me, you little fool." Furthermore, when we meet Rebecca, who appears fiercely independent, we find that certain characters in this novel loathe her for that very quality.

Overall, I did not find myself drawn to the brooding, jealous, and paranoid elements of this book, but I recognize that in other forms of media, painting, film, etc, may be very thrilling.

Title: The Hen Who Dreamed She Could Fly
Author: Sun-mi Hwang
My Review:
The Hen Who Dreamed She Could Fly by Sun-mi Hwang is a sweet tale of a hen who yearns to hatch an egg of her own. Sprout is a hen who can no longer lay healthy eggs and is removed from her chicken coop. Sprout is resilient, however, and through friendship and love is able to bring meaning into her life and survive many trials. This story is very short and sweet, but like a fable about motherhood, is one-dimensional and over-personified.

In the book, Sprout makes friends with Straggler, a mallard duck, who disappears from the farm. After surviving "The Hole of Death" thanks to Straggler's help, she finds that Straggler has gone missing. Sprout doesn't necessarily comprehend why Straggler has chosen to leave the farm to form a couple with another duck. Later, Sprout finds a thick briar patch and a blue egg, which she immediately takes to adopting. Straggler in the meantime delivers food to Sprout so she can care for the egg. When Straggler makes a ruckus to distract predators, and deliver food, Sprout doesn't seem to realize he is doing it selflessly for the egg.

The relationship Sprout has with her baby is also frustrating, as she notices that her baby wants to be part of the group of farm ducks. Out of fear for his safety, she limits his movements between that group and the wild.

Sprout is an example of the courage and resilience it takes to be a good mother, but exaggerates the story in a way that only shows Sprout's interpretation of what it means to be a good mother. During some scenes, we see Sprout finally understanding her world, but the last scene leaves us Sprout most of all wanting to be free of her hard life.

Title: The Hundred-Year-Old Man Who Climbed Out of the Window and Disappeared (The Hundred-Year-Old Man, #1)
Author: Jonas Jonasson
My Review:
This novel, written by Jonas Jonasson and published in 2009, describes the old man Allan Karlsson's recent adventure through Södermanland to Småland with an ever growing band of misfits. Parallel to his adventure, we learn about Allan's wild encounters with world leaders ranging from General Franco in Spain, to Truman in America, to Mao to Kim Il-sung and son Kim Jong-il in North Korea.

The theme of this book is that honesty may harm you but will also help you, that rules can always be broken, and that age can't limit you. The author supports these arguments by showing how well-liked Allan is by most people, by his genuineness and lack of ulterior motives (Allan mostly just asks for vodka whenever he wants something). We see that Allan breaks all kinds of rules (and the law) but he does so for the happiness of himself and his friends.

The book has helped me understand the political trends of the 20th century, in a comical and lenient way. However, at times I felt that some of the coincidences were too unbelievable - a bit like how Forrest Gump ends up meeting a lot of celebrities.

Overall, I recommend this book to anyone looking for a good laugh and a lighter read. Expect to laugh in the most unexpected moments and the humor to be whimsical - like when Allan insists he sees no point in why drinks should have parasol. The story will surely bring warmth to any worries you have about growing older.

Title: Market Wizards: Interviews with Top Traders (Market Wizards, #1)
Author: Jack D. Schwager
My Review:
Having been eager to get into investing while young, I found Market Wizards by Jack D. Schwager to be an enlightening collection of investing advice and trading advice. Schwager makes the distinction that investing means picking a collection of stocks that will bring long-term returns, while trading means studying price variations to make short-term returns.

The best and most common advice given from the book is to "do your homework" and this is emphasized by Schwager at the end, when he himself realizes that writing this book left him no time to study how to improve his trades. The next best advice was to "be flexible. Biases against certain markets or types of trades limit your field of opportunity".

My favorite investor interviewed after reading this book was Tom Baldwin. He emphasizes not viewing trading in terms of money and only using money to keep the score. Baldwin admits that "if you make a lot of money... you start to think you are infallible" and suggests not forgetting the research it took to make the good "picks". A good example of the fallibility of this goal is Mark Weinstein, who admits to wanting a castle in the south of France to enjoy and for capital appreciation. His wish to make a little more for the purchase $350,000 led him to wait too long on his trade, when it suddenly started decreasing.

This book provides expert advice to newcomers, and despite having a male-only perspective of being a trader, provides varied and interesting tips that are surely relevant in today's markets.

Title: The Bhagavad Gita
Author: Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa
My Review:
This explanation and overview of the Bhagavad Gita was released in 2007, as a second edition, by Eknath Easwaran. Recommended to me by an Indian friend, I was informed to use this author to guide me to the most essential ideas of Hinduism as I apply it to my personal life. After a brief introduction, the Gita opens to warrior Arjuna consulting his spiritual guide, Sri Krishna, for advice on how to win the battle of war, but also for self-realization. This book was one hundred percent effective at changing my worldview of India and of my place as a foreigner in my homeland.

The most important lessons I took away were: a) it is better to follow your individual path of karma in a mediocre way than to excel at someone else's destined bath, b) that death is only natural because everything that is alive must die, and everything that is dead will be born again. Death is only the unmanifested cycle of a soul.; c) obtaining knowledge of the self from within leads one to escape the cycle of being reborn. they who escape the "self" is not excited by good fortune, nor depressed by bad! There is pure joy in spiritual awareness.

It is important for westerners to note that what we learn as "yoga" is not just physical exercise. Instead, there are four paths of yoga - Karma Yoga, Bhakti Yoga, Raja Yoga and Jnana Yoga.

Some of the most powerful quotes I gathered from my readings that I will carry with me are: “Perform all work carefully, guided by compassion.” It inspires me to be a person more commited to service and the well-being of others in my community. In addition, I will keep a quote of when Vishnu decides to reveal his multi-armed form to convince the prince to do his duty: "I am become Time, the destroyer of worlds." Such a line invokes awe and humbleness in any reader.

Because of this literature, and the friend who has recommended this novel to me, I have become a more selfless person, and have placed less attachment on consumerist objects and my personal pleasure! I hope to embark on the path of Karma Yoga, renouncing the results of my personal actions as a spiritual offering.

Title: Watchmen
Author: Alan             Moore
My Review:
The Watchmen was published by DC comics in 1987 and of 12 chapters. It follows the story of the "Crimebusters" a band of masked vigilantes formed in 1966 and the second formed ever after the MinuteMen disbanded in 1949. The members of the group vary from Dr. Manhattan, a former technician who carrys beyond-physical powers to Nite Owl (Dan Dreiberg) and Silk Spectre II, characters with no special powers that were just continuations of those former personalities.

The craziness of these characters while they try to save humans around them lead to frequent confrontations. Dr. Manhattan has to face the possibility that he's made his colleagues sick with his special powers, Rorschach has to do what is right by any means possible, and the Nite Owl has to accept his passion for super-heroing to feel normal.

This graphic novel is excellent for its direct push to define morality: does killing people justify saving others? Is taking justice into your own hands ever a good idea in the long run? Beneath these giant questions of humanity the novel shows us themes of fear of Russians and nuclear attack. Readers who did not know the Cold War can get a sense of why Americans built up missile stocks - when your enemy is constantly getting stronger what choice do you have?

Lovers of comics will within a few pages be entranced by the passionate depictions of the characters; however, even those who appreciate a good story will make it to the end: a special plot twist guarantees it.

Title: Mind of the Raven
Author: Bernd Heinrich
My Review:
Mind of the Raven is an exploration of one researcher's observations of raven behavior over several years that explain raven intuition and intelligence. Bernd Heinrich is a professor emeritus in the biology department at the University of Vermont. Compared to other animal studies, this book takes a more intimate and thus revealing approach to ravens, with Heinrich having adopted ravens himself as well as having observed them in places like New England, Germany, Montana and Baffin Island in the high Arctic.

Giving insight to specific ravens he has known, we learn that Heinrich's personal interpratation is that ravens are contirdictory opporutnists who tend to form strong social bonds and are highly adaptable to their environments, thus achieving an intelligence related to their social environment. Overall, despite the observations being highly anectdotal, the detail with which Heinrich analyzes raven behavior is eye-opening. Heinrich states that "Intelligent behavior may result from a combination of curiosity, exploration, persistence, patience, keen observation, learning, and opportunism", claiming that intelligence physically is a complex connection of neuronal activity, while in practice it seems very similar to memory.

Heinrich's other observations of nature in general show a true respect and love for animal nature and hence human nature. When describing how a raven chooses a nesting location, he gives a very interesting (and accurate) definition for home: "To us, home is an area where we are at ease, because we are familiar with neighbors, with local peculiarities of food and shelter, and we recognize friends and potential enemies." As seen in any species, home is where we feel most safe. Another beautiful explanation is provided for fear: "A raven is afraid of what it knows to be dangerous, but that seems to be the least of its fears. Most of all, it is afraid of events that violate its expectations." According to this definition, creatures have certain expectations according to their experience and any breaking of that idea threatens their construct of the world.

Title: What a Carve Up! (The Winshaw Legacy, #1)
Author: Jonathan Coe
My Review:
What a Carve Up! is a satirical novel by Jonathan Coe, published originally in the UK in 1994. The novel is a satire on 1980's British politics and the Conservative government under Margaret Thatcher, which allowed for small, wealthy and powerful interest groups to take control in the nation. While making references to many other works, like What Carve UP! the film, as well as the novel The Ghoul, upon which the movie is based; The Death Lobby by Kenneth Timmerman. The main theme behind this book is the fine line between greed and madness.

During this novel, a young novelist called Michael Owen is commissioned to write a novel about the Winshaw family, a corrupt and greedy family whose own personal interests always spell disaster for other characters in the book. A different chapter is dedicated to each Winshaw relative: Hilary, a hypocritical tabloid columnist, Henry, a ruthless career politician, Dorothy, a brutal poultry and livestock farmer, Roderick, a sexually predatory art gallery owner, Thomas, an investment banker (who in himself is not so evil, except for being profit-obsessed), and finally Mark, an arms-dealer. Unfortunately, the last relative, Tabitha who spends her time in a mental asylum after the death of her brother, Godfrey.

Each of the characters, in particular the main character called Michael Owen, faces the choice between greed and madness. Michael ultimately commits his professional life to profiting greatly off the lives of a demented family by being paid to detail the life of the Winshaw family, only to find himself on the border of madness when documenting the stories of each Winshaw.

Michael appears to be mad in this novel, as he has recurring visions of a movie scene from What a Carve Up! as well of nightmares of falling from the sky, like Yuri Gagarin, and finally the image of an older man that ends up being himself. These visions end up being self-fulling and make him appear juvenile.

I enjoy the circularity of this novel, as it reminds me of the feeling of a good play, which introduces loose ends and ties them up in the end. In fact, I would be interested in seeing this novel as a play adaption. For theatre-lovers like myself, this novel plays on the rule of 3, that something is funnier when it happens three times. This novel has a high payout for those who pay attention to the details, as the end of the novel ties in the fate of Michael to previous plot details.

While it is clear that the author of this novel has experience with deja vu, and believing that everything is for a reason, circumstances of the novel prove that part of becoming an adult is accepting that one person is not always responsible for any one event, and that coincidence is a real part of the way the universe works.

Title: Open Veins of Latin America: Five Centuries of the Pillage of a Continent
Author: Eduardo Galeano
My Review:
Open Veins of Latin America: Five Centuries of the Pillage of a Continent was published in 1971 and is by Uruguayan journalist Eduardo Galeano. Galeano was working as an independent journalist when he wrote the book, which subsequently was banned by many right-wing military governments of Brazil, Chile, Argentina and Uruguay. Through fact gathering, Galeano presents the various developed nations of the time as conquistadors who at different times took the natural wealth out of Latin American land and people, leading to more dependent economies, exhausted soil, and unhealthy workers.

Each chapter focus on a different commodity that was particularly destructive to a country's economy. Those commodities included gold and silver, cacao and cotton, rubber and coffee, fruit, hides and wool, petroleum, iron, nickel, manganese, copper, aluminum ore, nitrates, and tin. The primary causes of destruction were a) a dependence on one commodity to provide financial stability, b) the protectionism of other nations, not allowing Latin Americans to enter the market and c) the profit concentration in the hands of intermediaries of foreign nationals (due to tax evasion and high margins, but not the local producers.

The book remains a very revealing source of Latin American history, regarding social and economic progress. The involvement of the US as a contract-maker was particularly interesting, seeing that it is often left out of school curriculum. However, certain sections feel too long, and the book may benefit from a reduction in length, as the most interesting pieces were often too short, while the lengthy discussion of the 'encomienda system' became too rambling.

Title: The Home and the World
Author: Rabindranath Tagore
Additional Authors: Surendranath Tagore, Anita Desai, William Radice
My Review:
Perhaps I don't know much about the Indian Nationalist Movement, which is why the book did not strike an emotional chord with me. I did however, appreciate the clarity of conflict all characters express within themselves (i.e. the choice to embrace Western culture or revolt against it).

A lot of the background happening in this book has to do with "Mussulman" groups. Most of the story I was left clueless as to what these groups had to with any of the story. Only upon doing some research did I learn about how the 1905 Partition of Bengal, which separated Muslims and Hindus, played a role in the Swadeshi movement of Indian natinoalism.

For the most part, I appreciate the story as a romance novel where Bimala, the main character, becomes infatuated with Sandip, a staunch supporter of anti-imperialism. Bimala gets so caught up with Sandip that she becomes willing to steal from her husband's accounts and spend large amounts of time with Sandip, listening to his speeches.

Bimala's irresponsibility and passionate obeisance to Sandip ultimately frustrates the reader, as we see her moving towards a path of self-destruction. Furthermore, dialogue with her sister-in-law (Senior Rani) over attention sought from Bimala's husband (Nikhil) is painful to read (but entirely realistic and thus wonderfully executed).

The main themes of the book were: clash of personality between Sandip (hot-headed, irrational) and Nikhil (cool-headed, reasonable), and the concept of "selling out" to foreigners versus "selling of conscience" by the locals.

Overall, the book is a tiring read for those not already familiar with India in the first decade of 1900. Some research prior to reading the book would be recommended.

Title: The Name of the Rose
Author: Umberto Eco
My Review:
Umberto Eco's The Name of the Rose was published in 1980 and consists of a tale told by a now aging Adso of Melk, a Benedictine monk from a German background. During the novel Adso recounts his brief stay at an unnamed abbey, whose setting is based off the real-life 10th-century Sacra di San Michele (near Torino, Italy).

During this time, a string of murders begin to occur regularly, nearly 1 a day, threatening the sanctity of the abbey and calling into question the authority of the abbot, named Abo, when famous inquisitors are called in to assess the mystery.

Surprising about the book is the what is likely accurate portrayal of medieval thinking: that women are "sinful creatures" and scientific thought has the ability to perverse trust in god. These passages can be distasteful to the female or scientific reader.

Fortunately, the presence of William of Baskerville, in charge of Adso's education, fuels a healthy does of reason and witty humor into the events of the novel. He is certainly comparable to a mixture of Sherlock Holmes and William of Ockham, a Franciscan friar and scholastic philosopher. His sleuthing is fascinating to observe for the long read, and perhaps with a 2nd read could be appreciated more.

The wish to name one character as murderer increases in the reader as time goes on. The tragedy occurring at the end of the novel strikes a blow to Adso and the audience, leaving meaning to the title in its final line. Essentially after witnessing the beauty of the abbey's design and the quality of its inward thought, all that exists of that treasure can only be held in its name.

In one additional thought, it has been neat discovering "easter eggs" of references made in this novel. Several reads would benefit the reader. My best find was "Jorge de Burgos", who after some research I realized was based off Jorge Luis Borges, the Argentine writer who became blind later in age. One of Borges' works called "The Library Of Babel" recalls a labyrinthine library with the quest for one book, likely influencing Umberto Eco in this novel.

Title: Preacher, Volume 6: War in the Sun
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
Preacher #34-40 and Preacher Special: One Man's War

Jesse Custer and the Saint of Killers meet up in Monument Valley so that Jesse can recruit him to kill God. Herr Starr, having taken over a new position of power, tries to kill the Saint of Killers - knowing that he will destroy Jesse Custer. Ultimately, Herr Starr detonates a nuclear missile, requiring Jesse and his friends to flee by plane. Jesse falls out of the plane and Tulip thinks her only love is dead.

This Volume had action on par with the events at Mesada. I loved the followup action to Mesada, knowing that Jesse is still alive - but all the parts having to do with Herr Starr were a bit dry - especially One Man's War.

Title: Preacher, Volume 9: Alamo
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
Preacher #59-66 closes out the comic book series and although it ties up all lose ends, was not as fascinating as some of the other editions.

In summary, Jesse makes a deal with the Saint of Killers to lure God away from his throne, so that upon return, the Saint of Killers is there with his plan for murder. Arseface, after becoming less popular, stays with Lorie, who due to having only one eye, finds him attractive.

Jesse has his showdown with Cassidy at the Alamo, and while they both come close to killing each other, ultimately Cassidy chooses to burn up at sunrise, and Jesse gets shot down by Herr Starr. Jesse, however, gets saved by God, although God ends up being confronted and killed. Finally Jesse and Tulip end up staying together.

The last two comics were 40 pages long and although this is understandable when you think of the comics as a finale, the lengthiness caused me tire out.

Title: Preacher, Volume 5: Dixie Fried
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
This Preacher Volume contains #27-33 and Preacher Special: Cassidy - Blood and Whiskey.

This is a powerful volume showing the evolution of Tulips character. Tulip gets propositioned by Cassidy and ties up Jesse for a whole day as punishment for having left her behind to fight at Mesada. She chooses to preserve Jesse's friendship with Cassidy.

We see that Arseface has a surprising vengeance against Jesse Custer who killed his father, the Sheriff. We learn that Jesse, needing to connect to Genesis, gets help from a voodoo expert Xavier. WE begin to suspect that Cassidy has let a lot of people down.

This Volume helps create a future for Arseface, which I enjoy, but the foreshadowing of Cassidy's betrayal was too developed; the majority of the focus of this Volume was about how terrible a person Cassidy just might be.

Title: Preacher, Volume 7: Salvation
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
Preacher 41 - 50 cover's Jesse recovery from falling from the plane, the discovery of his mom (now known as Jody, due to her memory loss from the violent confrontation with the real Jody) and confrontations with Odin Quincannon, the evil meat-packaging mogul from the town called Salvation.

Jesse is serving as a sheriff of Salvation. By the end of the series, he uses hallucinogens to finally process what happened when he fell out of the plane in Monument Valley. The experience finally encourages him to renew his quest to confront God.

The good points of these issues included Jesse bonding with his mom, but his experiences fighting Quincannon were tiresome and his total recall of his confrontation with god was exhausting.

Title: Preacher, Volume 8: All Hell's a-Coming
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
I love this part of the series! This part would be Preacher #51-58 and Preacher Special: Tall in the Saddle. We finally get to see Tulip's backstory in a way that how she grew up to be the lovable tomboy that she is. We also finally see Tulip come to her senses and ditch disgusting Cassidy.

In the last comic #58, we see Jesse come full circle and declare revenge on Cassidy for deceiving Jesse after he had trusted in him (and not to mention also taking advantage of Tulip).

The special Tall in the Saddle is very sweet and lets the reader learn the dynamic between Amy Grinderbinder, Tulip and Jesse. The prior two are best friends, and the latter two are lovers, and yet Amy and Jesse find a way to love each other in a platonic way despite their apparent attraction for each other.

Title: Preacher, Volume 3: Proud Americans
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
Preacher #18-26 shows Jesse learning about his father's service in Vietnam and Jesse and Tulip heading to Mesada. Jesse has a bad tendency to leave Tulip behind in order to save her from harm's way, and so Tulip often seems naive to Jesse's will. Allfather D'aronique's introduction in the story made me die laughing - his gluttony and his dull face seemed so immediatley disrespectful to the Catholic clergy; however, I recommend sticking to the comic if you're okay with religion having some fun poked out of it.

We meet Herr Star's ambition to find a new Messiah for the world. We learn about his distaste for "inbred bloodline" the Grail wishes to use to get the Messiah, and his plans to unseat the Allfather himself. We learn about Cassidy being captured at Mesada, and Jesse's determination to set him free - without Tulip intervening and getting hurt. Again, annoying to learn this habit of Jesse, but shows that Jesse has a machoist temperament.

The last of the volume ends with Cassidy's participation in the Easter Rising in 1916, but only to be rescued from certain death by his brother. While escaping, he gets bitten by an old women in a marsh and discovers he is sensitive to sunlight, and has become a vampire. I don't care much for Cassidy, but this was a good point of the story to place his history.

Title: Preacher, Volume 1: Gone to Texas
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
Preacher #1–7 comes up with a lot of imagination from the beginning - introducing the majority of characters starting from the very first comic - Saint of Killers, Jesse Custer, Tulip, Cassidy, the Adelphi and the Seraphi.

The main focus takes place as a recap of recent events in NYC that lead up to the trio Jesse, Tulip and Cassidy chatting it up in a Texas road stop/diner. Minor stories included Detective John Tool, the "unluckiest cop in the world" solving a Reaver-Cleaver case, with interwining connections to Cassidy. This volume ends with Jesse being told that his "grandmother" wants to see him in Angelville - with the image of dread on Jesse's face.

The visual clarity of the comic keeps me delighted at every page - with purple, grey hues in the illustration, violent drama and heart-shattering expressions, I found it hard to be bored. Unfortunately, a lot of character's traits have to be taken for granted, and one just has to remember as much as character's backstory as they can; the most difficulty I had was remembering how these characters relate to each other yet.

Title: Preacher, Volume 2: Until the End of the World
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
In Preacher #8–17 we find Jesse and Tulip fighting quite a bit with Tulip resenting Jesse's abandonment years ago, at the peak of their relationship. We find Jesse helping Tulip forget her current job of being a for-hire assassin, only for both to be caught by Jody, the main villain of Jesse's past. We learn of Jesse's backstory, the cruel upbringing he suffered at the hands of his "bloodline"/"blood of Jesus" obsessed grandmother.

I love these comics because we learn about Jesse's backstory and best of all, how Jesse and Tulip first met. As one fun detail, it seems the more Tulip gets to know Jesse, the longer she lets her hair grow? I always thought this to symbolize her growing trust with him.

Finally, we learn how much Tulip means to Jesse when she is lost to him, and revived by God. Additionally, we begin to suspect that God is a less-than-perfect and morally dubious - an interesting food for thought for those raised to believe in a God that is perfect.

While some people at this point will find the depiction of a selfish God blasphemous, if they've survived the violence and sex of this comic at this point, they probably won't stop reading now. I think its bold of Garth Ennis to suggest a story where God is blameworthy and i don't think his point is to disrespect religion, but rather to question the strictness and the seriousness (sometimes over seriousness) that we treat religion with.

Five stars!!

Title: Preacher, Volume 4: Ancient History
Author: Garth Ennis
My Review:
The fourth volume consists of Preacher Special: Saint of Killers #1-4, Preacher Special: The Story of You-Know-Who, and Preacher Special: The Good Old Boys.

The Story of Saint of Killers is the best one of this volume. We eagerly learn the details of the Saint of Killers, who serves as the Angel of Death to God - tasked with killing those who suffer violence. An ex-Confederate soldier, known for ruthless fighting, we discover is a cruel person as the result of a cruel life. We learn about the ten years of his life that were good, brought by a young bride he saved from a group of butchered Native Americans.

The Story of You-Know-Who reveals us the story of Arseface, who grew up with an alcoholic/distant mother and alcoholic/abusive father. He and his friend find such solace in Nirvana's Kurt Cobain, and loss of hope in their own difficult circumstances, that they take their own lives.

Finally, The Good Old Boys really deserves 3 stars because the characters Jody and T.C. are frankly completely reviling, and the whole comic focuses on their sex-obsessed habits and murdering tendencies.

Title: Alexander: Child of a Dream (Aléxandros, #1)
Author: Valerio Massimo Manfredi
My Review:
Alexander: Child of a Dream was written by Velrio Manfredi in 1998 and recounts the childhood and adolescence of Alexander the Great, who would later become a great military commander, expanding land from Greece to southern Asia.

As a big fan of historical fiction I can say that this book gives a good job relating the emotions that Alexander likely had every stage of life. For example, we can see that his distance from his mother Queen Olympia is due to a belief in her mysticism, that she speaks to the gods through animals and is connected to spirits. We also see that he has love for his sister Cleopatra, admiration of his father Phillip II, and deep loyalty to his friends.

Reading his story is inspiring to those who want to be influential in their communities and to the world. Those who follow his life in this novel will find evidence that Alexander enjoyed comparing himself to Achilles, half-God and half-human, as did his friends.

While Alexander faces threats to his throne for a short time towards the end, due to his young age and supposed lack of experience, his ambition and the loyalty of his friends guarantees him security.

Title: Shantaram
Author: Gregory David Roberts
My Review:
Shantaram is a fictional novel by [a:Gregory David Roberts|18907|Gregory David Roberts|https://images.gr-assets.com/authors/1252694281p2/18907.jpg], published in 2003. The novel follows the story of an Australian escaped convict and ex-heroin addict who moves to Bombay (renamed Mumbai when the Shiv Shena - valuing Maratha heritage - came to power in 1995 and changed the name to strengthen the Marathi identity). The author wrote the story loosely based around his own life; after his marriage fell apart, he became addicted to heroin and robbed banks to fuel his addiction. Roberts himself has said in a BBC interview that he wrote Shantaram during the rest of his prison sentence, and that during this time prison wardens destroyed his manuscript twice.

Shantaram is about the goodness other people bring out in you, and the anger one can produce in himself. In this novel, we learn that Roberts is a highly emotional person and deeply loyal, with respect for genuine, hard-working people, regardless of their status (like slum families and farmers) and hatred towards cruel, powerful people who use their power for selfish motives, (like some gangsters and prison wardens). When Roberts meets a village family, they give him the name "Shantaram" meaning "man of God's peace", either believing his heart to be good, or planting the idea, end letting him grow into a person of peace.

The best of Bombay is truly highlighted in this novel, and never having seen Bombay myself, I felt truly immersed in the smells of cooking, colors of clothing, and sights of religious worship that Roberts provides us. It is important to note, however, that in the novel, we can only experience Bombay through the eyes of a criminal, who produces false passports and prints money. To know whether this gives an incomplete image of the city (showing only the ugly underside), or rather a truly rounded one (with the good and the bad), one would have to travel to the city today, to determine that for himself.

Title: The Tortilla Curtain
Author: T. Coraghessan Boyle
My Review:
The book The Tortilla Curtain is a profound look into the lives of upper-class families in the U.S. and the stark contrast with migrant families looking for work in the U.S. The struggles of upper-class to preserve their wealth contrasts starkly with the struggles of migrant families to get work. Interestingly, another major struggle in the book is the struggle of humans against nature, be it natural disasters like fires, and mudslides, or wildlife. Another major struggle is that of man against man, of humans fighting to have their own space free of other humans. While the details of daily life of both migrants and locals was very interesting, the increasing pessimism and disaster of the book was devastating to the reader and too bleak to convey any message beyond 'life is hard'.

The book starts with an accident in which Delaney Mossbacher (self-declared a liberal humanist) first faces a Mexican-born man living in Topanga Canyon. Delaney cycles through many emotions when he realizes he has hit the man (Candido), being moved from guilt to anger to outrage. Delaney becomes ultimately angry because he feels that the immigrants who are occupying the public land are harming the nature that belongs to everyone. Delaney represents the privileged class that intend well, but occasionally feel threatened by the presence of others. Together with his wife they are "perfectionist...abhorred clutter...were joggers, non-smokers, social drinkers".

Candido has recently migrated to the US having narrowly escaped the border crossing with his wife America, who is a young, 17-year old girl. Candido prides himself in his work, and is ashamed to be injured from a traffic accident and unable to work. Candido has the most hopeful encounters with humans of all characters in the book, with the best quote being "Life may be inveterately grim and the surprises disproportionately unpleasant, but it would be hardly worth living if there were no exceptions, no sunny days, no acts of random kindness." (pg.170).

The interaction that humans in this book have with nature pushes the reader to see that Delaney ultimately wishes to defend his belongings, while Candido ultimately wishes the opportunity to acquire these belongings for himself. The coyote is definitely a metaphor for the migrant worker who is seen as a raider and having large families. People who are too generous in the novel are often described as encouraging the 'coyotes' to take what they want. However, Delaney says that "the coyote is not to blame - he is only trying to survive." (pg. 214). Others believe that the coyote is "cunning, versatile, hungry and unstoppable" (pg.215), certainly traits of determination that Candido shows when he looks for food, shelter and safety for his family.

The book ends on a very negative note, with significant loss to the migrant family. While the reader can hope that the beliefs that Delaney has shown, such as wanting to respect nature and giving everyone a fair chance, we see that in reality his actions reveal that migrant families may be ultimately doomed to isolation and lack of opportunity, according to this author.

Title: The Book Thief
Author: Markus Zusak
My Review:
The Book Thief is an extremely engaging story for an avid reader, as it tells the story of a young girl who is in love with reading. It is no surprise the book is a bestseller, as it appeals to precisely the kind of person who would read a book. The Book Thief by Markus Zusak is a historical novel published in 2005. The reading level can be described as for young adults as some vocabulary is in German, high fluency is needed to retain the various scenes that are presented in the book, and because differing perspectives of the characters requires critical thinking.

The story is about a young girl called Liesel Meminger who is placed into foster care of an energetic couple, the Hubermanns. Liesel moves into their home in Molching, Germany (a fictional place) just before the German invasion of Poland, which led Britain and France to declare war on Hitler's Nazi state. Liesel during the war falls in love with reading and books, in general, and builds a strong connection to her family, her neighbors, and a surprise guest in their house.

The most powerful character in this novel, is Death, who breaks the fourth wall in his narration by commenting on the character's actions, such as when he judges Liesel for struggling with death for the first time: "Why do they always shake them? Yes, I know, I know, I assume it has something to do with instinct." Death describes himself as a hard-worker who gets especially fatigued during war. He describe war like "a new boss who expects the impossible... the boss, however, does not thank you. He asks for more."

One of the main themes of the novel is fear. Liesel is constantly in fear that her the people she loves most will be taken away. This may be due to the shock of leaving her biological mother and biological brother, but it also may be assumed to be natural as the war causes unpredictability. The word for fear in the novel is angst. Liesel feels angst when her foster father Hans is sent to work for the LSE (the air force team), when Max is in their basement while the Nazis go door to door looking for appropriate LSR (air raid shelters), and not least of all, when stealing books.

In the end a respect for words leads to a respect for the situation that Liesel has lived through. Although she feels that the power of words have destroyed her life - the hateful words of Hitler caused a nation to falsely desire war, she ultimately believes that words saved her life, by giving her a tool to communicate her friendship to Max, and occupy her free time while war was being waged. Death himself, despite his ominous presence, is left in awe of the Book Thief's story, admiring the way she captured the horrors and the blessings of surviving Nazi Germany.

Title: Maus: A Survivor's Tale II: And Here My Troubles Began
Author: Art Spiegelman
My Review:
While Maus I ends as an obvious cliff-hanger, Maus II ties up the loose ends. Art Spiegelman shows incredible passion, caution and care in dealing with his father's story.

In this second chapter, we see an aging Vladek help Artie finish documenting how the Holocaust ended. This portion contains more vivid (and therefore gruesome) details of Auschwitz, but nothing that disrupts the flow of Vladek's story.

As the chronology continues, we see how Vladek escapes more and more dangerous situations. Despite being incredibly intelligent, Vladek leaves the reader with the impression that luck is the most important instrument to survival.

Just as in Maus I, the experiences Artie has with his father and mother-in-law are an interesting offset to the extreme heartache that is the Holocaust. At some moments, we worry for Vladek's physical health, just as we worry for Artie's mental health. But as the story concludes, we realize that familial loves overcomes any of the character's difficult moments.

Title: Norwegian Wood
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
Norweigan Wood, originally published in 1987, was first translated into English by Alfred Birnbaum as a text for Japanese students of English. However, This review regards the 2nd English translation, by Jay Rubin, which was published in 2000.

In this book, we watch as Watanabe, the main character, attends university in Tokyo in the late 1960's, during a time of revolt. As he attends classes, he develops long-term commitments and deep relationships to people around him. For those familiar with psychosocial theory and Erik Erikson's work in 1959, this is very reminiscent of the 6th stage of development, that of Intimacy vs. Isolation.

We see that after losing a friend from high school, Watanabe forms a close bond to his dead friend's girlfriend in college. While his relationship her grows complicated, due to her ever-worsening depression, Watanabe finds himself moving towards a new relationship full of life and friendship, in a girl named Midori.

Overall, the book will be comforting to those who have suffered crises in their lives. Unfortunately, the simplicity of diction will probably lead to a faster reading, and less appreciation of the slow development of the relationships. Despite this issue, the experiences painted by the author are capitivating and are so detailed as to appear auto-biographical.

My favorite message taken away from this book is that mental illness in a relationship is unforgiving, but memories will always be a treasure and a comfort to those who are suffering.

Title: The Brothers Karamazov
Author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
My Review:
The Brothers Karamazov was the final novel written by Fyodor Dostoyevsky and also his largest work, at almost 800 pages. The novel was published in the year 1880.

This novel mainly focuses on patricide of an older man who has three sons off of two marriages. However, at times the novel focuses on philosophical arguments given by Father Zosima to Alyosha as well as side stories of the youngest son, Alyosha, the middle child, Ivan, and the oldest son, Dmitri, as well as the suspect to go on trial.

During the course of the novel, we learn that the wealthy woman Katarina Ivanovna has been engaged to Dmitri, the eldest son, described as a big spender, an ex-military man and a person of overall "violent emotion". We learn, however, that Dmitri falls for Grushenka (Agrafena Alexandrovna), a beautiful enchantress left to lodge at the widow Morosov's house by her master Samsonov. We find that by her beauty or wit, she also steals the heart of Fyodor Pavlovitch, the greedy, almost malicious Karamazov father.

After the violent murder one night of Fyodor, we see that detective Perhotin (Pyotor Ilyitch) immediately begins to gather evidence against Dmitri, while the officer Mavriky Mavrikyevitch is sent to Mokroe to get Dmitri before he shoots himself. Amongst the most incriminating evidence
is the brass pestle he picks up before visiting his father to look for Grushenka.

Not being an expert in religion or politics might make someone lose track of some of the arguments, but I could usually understand the message by the end of the chapter. One example is the discussion of socialism - many characters seem to have widely different opinions about socialism, without an explanation of what socialism is. However, we do see the quote that socialism is ''the question of the tower of Babel built without God, not to mount to heaven from earth but to set up heaven on earth''. This to me casts this policy or practice negatively, as something too much for humans to aspire to.

The best part of the book were the beautiful quotes. Unfortunately, to make it to the best quotes, the reader will have to have the stamina to get through detailed passages that one wonders why the author included.

Title: Extremely Loud & Incredibly Close
Author: Jonathan Safran Foer
My Review:
Extremely Loud and Incredibly close is a novel by author Jonathan Foer, published in 2005. The author deals with the relatively new subgenre of 9/11 fiction, telling the story of 9/11 from not only from the perspective a New Yorker, but also a child. The purpose of the book is to show how Oskar Schell handles adversity with the strength of family and the power of humor.

When Oskar goes searching for the origin of an envelope with the name "Black" on it, we slowly learn of different people of different age groups and life experiences. Oskar makes friends with an old man named Mr. A. R. Black who keeps biography cards on people he wants to remember. My favorite quote of the book is when Mr. Black says "Nine out of ten significant people have to do with money or war!". Later, when Mr. Black suspects they are being followed, he protects Oscar without letting Oscar know.

Later, we see Oskar meet Abby Black, who lives in a narrow house and is extremely sad and beautiful. We see that Oskar flirts with Abby in a humorous way, by asking if he can kiss her, and referring to her beauty by noting her "huge boobs". While Oskar uses incredible courage in meeting strangers, perhaps it's humor more than bravery he relies on to face people.

Overall, the book is incredibly entertaining for its creative use of media: this book is not only text, but also photos from Oskar's journal, letters from his grandmother and interactive phone dialogue. However, the discussion of two major tragedies, the bombing of civilians Dresden and the attack of 9-11, might be extremely painful to process for one novel. Additionally, while Oskar's story is incredibly approachable, one must wonder what the story would be like from Oskar's mother's perspective, which is never explored.

Title: East of Eden
Author: John Steinbeck
My Review:
The most explored themes in literature and other media is the battle between good and evil, sometimes seen as man versus man, but very often as man versus himself. While East of Eden by John Steinbeck presents us with three generations of a family of brothers that battle one another, the overarching struggle we see is the argument that an individual has with himself, namely, Adam's seeking for perfection, and Caleb's acceptance of his "badness".

I was concerned that the evil characters in this book would be portrayed one-dimensional. However, the close observation of Cathy Ames reveals that Steinbeck understands the complexity of bad-acting characters. Cathy displays sociopathy, a lack of empathy of others and the need to protect herself at all costs. Cathy herself comes to this realization in the novel, after years of thinking other people strange. Steinbeck says "As a child may be born without an arm, so one may be born without kindness or the potential of conscience." Thus, instead of assuming Cathy is pure evil, the violence and abandonment of responsibility shown by Cathy was given a cause.

Anyone who has grown up with complicated familial or friendship ties will benefit from this novel, as it explores the idea of second chances and innate personality traits of problematic people. The reader comes away from the book having new faith in humanity, reflected by the Hebrew word "Timshel", that gives a choice to be good or bad. It is clear that Steinbeck from start to finish of the novel is a person who likes humans, saying "But I have a new love for that glittering instrument, the human soul." An underrated but important point about this quote is that the soul is an instrument, and thus can be used for whatever purpose it may, good or bad.

Steinbeck is a master at painting the American spirit in this novel, which at certain points of history can be seen as lying, thieving but also relentless, ambitious and energetic. "All colors and blends of Americans have somewhat the same tendencies. It’s a breed—selected out by accident. And so we’re overbrave and overfearful—we’re kind and cruel as children." In the characters of soldiers, businessmen, inventors and prostitutes, we see an excess of energy in this novel that captures perfectly my greatest fears but also my greatest desires.

I can see myself returning to this novel again and again when I need a renewed boost of faith in people. This book took me years to finish, because of the direct exposure to the ugly facets of human psyche, and the fear i had of being that close to jealousy, passion and hate. However, I knew that finishing this novel would pay off because for all the sharp edges of its characters, it offered me the promise of opportunity of choosing what kind of person I want to be.

Title: The Prophet
Author: Kahlil Gibran
My Review:
Khalil Gibran published The Prophet in 1923 and is one of the most translated books in history. In the book, we explore the mystical meaning of life through the words of a prophet called Almustafa, who is about to leave the city of Orphalese after 12 years. Each chapter is a different commentary on one facet of life, regarding intangible things like freedom, pain, and beauty, but also tangible things like houses and clothes.

Khalil's work feels more like poetry, and when translated to Spanish, for example, can sound very formal. The spiritual mysticism of each text is evident, and suggests to the reader that the key to happiness or success is acceptance of one's self. In small snippets, Khalil provides what feels like the wisdom of an old man, who has seen the world, and despite his troubles has no regrets.

If this book teaches me anything, it is that being humble is the key to being happy. In a quote the prophet says "Say not, 'I have found the truth,' but rather,'I have found a truth'". The prophet accepts that you can never really know everything there is to know about life. In another, he says, "For in the dew of little things the heart finds its morning and is refreshed." While advertising and popular culture may lead someone to think that possessions, or quantity of happiness, or quantity of knowledge is an important goal, these quotes suggest accepting the truth that one has, as well as cherising the little moments one has.

This book of poetry will continue to be a classic to be read at every birth, marriage and funeral, and arguably crosses any divisions of religion. Khalil, after all, was born a Maronite Christian but was heavily influenced by Sufism. If Khalil was able to capture the human spirit as a Christian and a Muslim, than readers of any religion will surely be able to relate.

Title: The Richest Man in Babylon
Author: George S. Clason
My Review:
The Richest Man in Babylon is a book written by George S. Clason and published in 1926 that offers a set of parables centered on the generation and accumulation of wealth, luck and opportunity. I was recommened this book by the Google Search engine when researching classic books about finance. Unfortunately, I give this book 3 stars because the advice provided in 144 pages could have easily been summed up in 2 pages, an in addition, the interesting setting of Babylon is not entertaining enough to warrant such droning of language.

The main points to be summarized from this novel are: a) if you desire to aid a friend with a loan, find ways to guarantee reimbursement, as not to burden oneself; b) wealth only stays with people who have knowledge and purpose; c) luck only comes to those who work hard; d) save 10% of everything you earn; and e) make those savings "work for you" by earning interest in investments. I wasn't sure why this novel was so obsessed with the idea of 10%, and may be arbitrary, since what I'm used to hearing about is the 50/30/20 budgeting rule.

In addition, perhaps by being a book from almost 100 years ago, I found it upsetting that no parables were given about women who desired to build savings or women entrepreneurs.

Overall, the book is valuable for common themes of fiscal responsibility, but remains severly outdated when compared to the modern world. Everything learned here in this book can likely be found much faster by listening to a radio show, podcast, or reading a magazine article. The entertainment factor was limited because the book is an advice piece, with little plot or character development.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring (The Lord of the Rings, #1)
Author: J.R.R. Tolkien
My Review:
Having watched The Lord of the Rings in animated form, I am naturally biased to love this first chapter of the trilogy.

Reading this book for the second time, I still see this as the best of the three works. All the Shire imagery and Elf imagery sets up the universe for us, the reader.

This first book has characters trekking through the safest parts of Middle Earth (exceptions made for Weathertop HIll and Caradhras). We see the characters experience interesting and diverse locations (in order - The Great Forest, Bree (and Mr. Butterbur's Inn), Rivendell, Dimrill Dale, the Naith of Lorien, and the City of Galadhrim).

Just looking at the book has been useful to figuring out what was left out of the movies - e.g. wolf-like wargs exist in the universe and have to be fought off near Weathertop, and the closest Frodo and the Hobbits ever come to death in the series arguably happens when the Hobbits meet a barrow-wight just out of the Old Forest (anyone reminded of GoT wights?).

Reading this book has been an exercise of the mind because the quantity of names, objects and people requires a lot of brain space; on the other hand, we are left truly convinced that this universe could be real; and unlike action scenes in the LoTR movies, the action scenes in the book are more exciting than they are tedious.

This is a must read and is good for any fiction lover, especially science fiction and fantasy. The book is also suitable for children (recommended for the adventure-loving).
